What makes a microservice truly "independently deployable" (its own codebase/pipeline, private database, backward-compatible contracts, no shared-library lockstep), and why is independent deployability — not size — the real test of whether you have microservices or a distributed monolith?

Given a monolithic (e.g. food-delivery) application, how would you decompose it into microservices (DDD bounded contexts, database-per-service, extract one module at a time), and what challenges do you face?
Explain the Decomposition design pattern (by business capability, by subdomain/DDD, by transaction, by scalability).
Explain Bounded Context in microservices (DDD), its principles, advantages, and disadvantages.

How do you use Event Storming to decompose a domain (map commands/triggers → aggregates/state-managers → domain events/outcomes with domain experts), and what are the rules for designing aggregate roots at high TPS — keep aggregates SMALL (a "god" aggregate causes severe optimistic-locking contention), treat the aggregate as the consistency/transaction boundary, and reference OTHER aggregates by ID only (never by direct object reference) so boundaries stay clean and extractable into separate services?

What are the DDD tactical building blocks and how do they map to Java/Spring code — Entity, Value Object, Aggregate, Repository, Domain Service, Application Service — and what are the strategic DDD concepts: Bounded Context, Ubiquitous Language, Context Mapping, and Domain Events?

When should two microservices be MERGED back (or decomposition stop) — when the boundary creates coordination without autonomy (same team, deployed together, synchronous chains, shared consistency, lockstep schema/API changes), and why should a healthy architecture be able to delete/merge services, not only create them?
How do microservices communicate (synchronous REST/Feign/gRPC vs asynchronous Kafka/RabbitMQ), and when do you use each?
When do you choose a REST API over Kafka/messaging queues and vice versa?
What are the differences between REST, gRPC, and Kafka?
Which design pattern is used for synchronous communication between microservices (API Gateway)?

Why is the N+1 problem not just a Hibernate issue but a general distributed pattern (1 initial call + N dependent calls — e.g. fetch 100 users then call another service once per user = 1 + 100 network calls), why is the network version often worse than the DB version (higher latency, more failure modes), and how do you fix it (batch/bulk endpoints, a single aggregated call, caching, parallel fan-out with bounded concurrency)?
What is an API Gateway, its functions (routing, aggregation, auth, rate limiting, load balancing, caching, logging, fault tolerance), and when to use it?
Explain the API Gateway pattern and its responsibilities.
When a request reaches the gateway and the target service is down, how do you handle it (circuit breaker, fallback, cache, retry/backoff, service discovery, feature flags)?
How do you dynamically route requests to different backends at runtime in Spring Cloud Gateway (`RouteLocator`)?
How do you handle request aggregation in an API Gateway when multiple services must be queried (parallel WebClient + `Mono.zip`)?
How does an API Gateway handle caching, and what problems arise (stale data, granularity, caching sensitive data)?
How does an API Gateway track request tracing across microservices (trace IDs, Zipkin/OpenTelemetry)?
How can an API Gateway enforce zero-trust security principles (mTLS, OAuth2/JWT, dynamic access control, anomaly detection)?
How would you prevent replay attacks in an API Gateway (nonce, dedupe within a time window via Redis)?
How do you implement multi-tenancy in an API Gateway?
What is a shadow deployment, and how do you implement it?
How do you implement blue-green deployments in an API Gateway (weighted routing)?

Why does an API Gateway become the system's CPU bottleneck and single point of failure under high load (every request pays for JSON parsing, JWT verification, an auth call, a rate-limit check, synchronous logging, transformation, and a new upstream connection), and what is the guiding rule to fix it (do as little work as possible on the request path — move non-critical work off it, cache aggressively, never do synchronous I/O in the request handler)?

How do you offload authentication so JWT verification stops saturating the gateway (local verification with cached public keys in a sidecar, a dedicated auth tier that issues a pre-verified context token the API tier trusts, or a short-TTL token-introspection cache), and why is ECDSA verification cheaper than RSA?

How do you cut per-request overhead at the gateway — connection pooling / HTTP/2 multiplexing to reuse upstream connections instead of a new TCP+TLS handshake each time (target >99% connection reuse), hybrid rate limiting (a local token bucket synced to Redis every ~100ms instead of a Redis round trip per request), async batched logging off the request path, and request coalescing (de-duplicate identical in-flight requests)?
What is the difference between a Service Registry and Service Discovery?

Explain service discovery in depth — service registry, instances, clients, client-side vs server-side discovery, health checks, load balancing/failover, Kubernetes DNS, service mesh, security (registry poisoning, mTLS/Zero Trust), performance (DNS TTL, proxy hops, registry scaling), and multi-region setups.
If one microservice is down, how do you handle it gracefully (circuit breaker, fallback, retry with backoff, timeout, bulkhead, graceful degradation, monitoring)?
If you have two instances of a service and both crash, how do you make the service fault tolerant (multi-node, Kubernetes self-healing, auto-scaling, health checks, multi-zone)?
How do you keep the application available during a huge surge in traffic (horizontal scaling, auto-scaling, caching, async processing, DB scaling, monitoring)?
How do you know a service is up and running (health endpoints, heartbeats, service registry, Kubernetes probes, monitoring, gateway checks)?
How do you achieve fault isolation (exception handling, circuit breaker, redundancy, microservice boundaries, failover, bulkhead, resource limits)?
What is scaling, and what is the difference between vertical scaling (scale up) and horizontal scaling (scale out)?
How do you scale a microservices application (horizontal/vertical scaling, load balancing, API gateway, containers/orchestration, DB scaling, async, auto-scaling, monitoring, circuit breaker)?

How do you evolve an architecture from 1 user to 1M+ users as each component becomes the bottleneck (optimize queries/indexes → stateless app + load balancer → cache + read replicas + CDN → async message queue + rate limiting → microservices/sharding → auto-scaling + multi-region), and why is the principle "start simple → measure → find the bottleneck → scale → repeat"?

Why should you first clarify what "1 million users" means (registered vs daily-active vs concurrent) before designing, since the real driver is requests/sec, read/write ratio, data size, and latency/consistency requirements?

What is the difference between Kubernetes HPA (more/fewer replicas by load), VPA (adjust a pod's CPU/memory), and Cluster Autoscaler (add/remove nodes), can HPA and VPA be used together safely, and when do you reach for event-driven/queue-based scaling (KEDA — e.g. scale workers by queue depth rather than CPU)?
If you have N instances, how do you distribute requests equally (load balancer algorithms, health checks, Kubernetes Service)?
Explain the Load Balancer and the Rate Limiter — what each does, their algorithms, and the tools used.
How do you implement per-user rate limiting in a distributed environment (Redis + token/leaky bucket, Bucket4j, gateway)?

Compare the rate-limiting algorithms — fixed-window counter (simple but allows a ~2× burst at the window boundary), sliding-window log/counter (smooths that boundary burst at higher memory cost), token bucket (allows controlled bursts up to the bucket size with steady refill), and leaky bucket (enforces a constant outflow rate) — and how do you enforce the limit consistently across many instances (a shared counter in Redis)?
How is a load balancer implemented in Azure (Azure Load Balancer L4, Application Gateway L7, Front Door global, AKS LoadBalancer service)?
How do you trace a request across multiple microservices (distributed tracing, correlation IDs, centralized logging)?

Why are technical trace IDs alone insufficient for long-running async workflows, and why do you also propagate a durable business identifier (orderId, paymentId, workflowId) so you can reconstruct an operation hours later after individual traces expire?

Why can every service look healthy (green health checks, normal CPU, low error rate) while the product is actually broken, and why do you need end-to-end business metrics and synthetic journeys (order-completion rate, payment-success rate) rather than only per-service dashboards?
How do you design and choose databases for microservices (database-per-service, SQL vs NoSQL vs Redis, scalability/consistency factors)?
What is the difference between a single shared database and the database-per-service approach?
How is data consistency handled in a distributed microservices architecture (strong vs eventual, Saga, event-driven, 2PC, outbox)?

What is two-phase commit (2PC/XA) — the prepare (voting) phase then the commit phase coordinated by a transaction coordinator — why is it a blocking protocol (if the coordinator crashes after everyone votes YES, participants hold locks indefinitely), and why do most microservice architectures prefer a Saga + eventual consistency over 2PC?

What is the Two Generals Problem (two parties over an unreliable channel can never reach GUARANTEED agreement because any ack can be lost), and how does it map to real distributed systems (a payment/settlement across banks can't be made perfectly atomic over the network) — so instead of pretending certainty you design for it with acknowledgements + retries + idempotency + reconciliation and accept eventual consistency?

Why can't you rely on wall-clock timestamps to order events across distributed nodes (clock skew / drift means node A's "later" timestamp may precede node B's "earlier" one), and how do logical clocks fix ordering — Lamport clocks for a total/causal order, vector clocks to detect concurrency, and HYBRID LOGICAL CLOCKS (HLC) which combine physical time with a logical counter to give monotonic, causally-consistent, human-readable timestamps for ordering financial events?

What is the dual-write problem (writing to the database and publishing to Kafka as two separate steps can leave them inconsistent if one fails), and how does the Transactional Outbox pattern solve it (write the domain change and an event row to an `outbox` table in the same local DB transaction, then a separate relay — polling or Change Data Capture via Debezium tailing the DB log — publishes those rows to Kafka with at-least-once delivery)?

What is the difference between a DOMAIN event (internal to one bounded context, triggers side effects across aggregates, often via an in-process event bus like Spring Application Events) and an INTEGRATION event (published to Kafka for cross-service communication), and why must integration events act as an Anti-Corruption Layer — exposing only a stable, versioned schema (Avro/Protobuf + Schema Registry) and keyed by the aggregate-root ID for per-aggregate ordering — rather than leaking the producer's internal model?

What is the difference between Event Notification (a minimal event carrying just an id + event name + a link to fetch details) and Event-Carried State Transfer (the event carries the data consumers need), what is the "fat event / god event" anti-pattern (broadcasting the whole aggregate "just in case"), and how do you decide between the two (coupling vs extra calls, with versioned schemas either way)?

Should every microservice publish an event for every database change — no, events are CONTRACTS that create dependencies just like APIs — publishing every table mutation as a public event stream exposes persistence internals, makes schema evolution painful, and couples consumers to the producer's internal model — instead, publish events representing meaningful DOMAIN FACTS that other components legitimately need, and treat the event schema as a versioned integration contract (not a DB changelog)?

If instance App1 updates a value, how does instance App2 see the change (there is no shared JVM memory) — via a shared database as the source of truth, a distributed cache like Redis, or a Kafka event that other instances consume to update local state/invalidate caches?
In a Search/Order/Payment/Delivery system, if the payment fails, how do you manage consistency using the Saga pattern and compensating actions instead of `@Transactional`?
What is the difference between choreography and orchestration?

What is the "pinball architecture" / chained-choreography anti-pattern (a complex multi-step workflow modeled purely as reactive events chained across many services with no coordinator), why is it dangerous (you can't observe the workflow state or handle compensations), and when should you switch to an orchestrated Saga with a central state machine (e.g. Spring State Machine / Temporal / Camunda) that owns the steps and compensating transactions?
How do you implement rollback in a Saga pattern using orchestration?
What is Event Sourcing (store events not state, replay to reconstruct state), its advantages, disadvantages, and example?

Explain CQRS (Command Query Responsibility Segregation) and when to use it — separate the write model (command side: receives commands, enforces business rules via aggregates, emits domain events) from the read model (query side: denormalized projections optimized for specific query shapes) — and why does this separation help (write model optimized for consistency/invariants, read model optimized for query performance without fat joins or full aggregate loading, each side scales independently)?

How do you implement CQRS in a Spring Boot service without a framework like Axon — Commands as immutable records/DTOs, an Aggregate (e.g. `Order`) that encapsulates state transitions and emits Domain Events (e.g. `OrderPlacedEvent`, `OrderShippedEvent`), Command Handlers that load the aggregate and invoke its methods, a Write Repository (JPA) for the aggregate, a Projection/Event Listener that consumes domain events (via `@EventListener` or `@TransactionalEventListener`) and updates a separate Read Model (a denormalized entity/table optimized for queries), a Read Repository for the read model, and two separate controllers (one for commands, one for queries) — and why is this "clean architecture" approach maintainable without the complexity of a full event-sourcing framework?

What are the CQRS trade-offs — benefits (independent scaling of reads/writes, optimized read models, simpler write logic focused on invariants, easier to add new query shapes without touching the domain) vs costs (eventual consistency between write and read models, data duplication, more code/infrastructure, projection rebuild complexity) — and when should you NOT use CQRS (simple CRUD apps, low traffic, when strong consistency between write and read is required on every request, when the team doesn't need independent read/write scaling)?

Why did the industry move beyond synchronous REST for long-running workflows (thread blocking, thread-pool exhaustion, HTTP 202 Accepted, accept-then-process), and what does async communication actually improve?
What happens if a service crashes during an update using asynchronous communication, and how do you handle it (ack+retry, idempotency, DLQ, transactional outbox, circuit breaker, saga)?
Explain the execution flow of a parent task that spawns multiple child tasks and combines their results.

How do you migrate a live workflow from synchronous REST to Kafka without a flag-day cutover — let both models coexist, define which is authoritative at each stage, use shadow/dual processing + idempotent consumers + feature flags to validate the event path, then transfer ownership gradually without losing or duplicating business operations?
What is idempotency, which HTTP methods should be idempotent, and why does it matter?

What are the different ways to implement idempotency and when do you use each — idempotency keys (payments: store key→response, return the stored response on retry), DB unique constraints (prevent duplicate records), state-based validation (skip if the resource is already in the target state), and distributed locks (one-time coupon under high concurrency)?

(Scenario) A race condition causes the SAME payment to be processed twice — how do you prevent it end to end (idempotency key per request, a unique DB constraint on the transaction id, transaction management, a distributed lock only where truly needed, atomic operations), and crucially how do you handle client/payment-provider RETRIES so a retry returns the original stored result instead of charging again?

(Scenario) What happens if the application crashes AFTER a payment succeeds but BEFORE the response reaches the client (the client retries, risking a double charge), and why does this make server-side idempotency — not client discipline — the only safe design?

(Scenario) A product manager wants the UI to show "payment confirmed" BEFORE the transaction is durably committed — why is this dangerous (the commit can still fail/roll back, so you've told the user something false), and what do you propose instead (confirm only after the durable commit; for long-running work return a `202 Accepted` + a pending/processing state the client polls or gets notified about, with the confirmation driven by the real committed outcome)?

How do you implement concurrency control for the "last item / last ticket" problem as a progression — `synchronized`/`ReentrantLock`/`AtomicInteger`/`ConcurrentHashMap` (single JVM only) → DB optimistic/pessimistic locking → Redis distributed lock (`SETNX` + TTL) across many instances → a queue that serializes requests to one consumer (no locks needed)?

How do you make a message/event consumer safe against at-least-once duplicate delivery (store a `processed_event_id` / inbox table and skip already-processed IDs, use unique DB constraints, or idempotent state transitions) — and why is "do not corrupt state on reprocessing" the real goal rather than literal exactly-once?

Why does a naive `if (!alreadyProcessed(id)) { process(); markProcessed(id); }` dedup still double-process under concurrency or on crash, and what are the two fixes — make the dedup write atomic (`INSERT ... ` with a `UNIQUE(event_id)` constraint so only one consumer wins) and commit the business update and the dedup record in the SAME database transaction (so a crash after the update but before marking cannot cause reprocessing to re-apply it)?

How do you handle a hot row that many requests update at once (e.g. a shared like/stock counter) — counter sharding (split into N sub-counters and sum) or buffering increments in Redis and periodically syncing to the DB?
What are the strategies for API versioning, what are the tradeoffs, and how do you change a widely used API without breaking existing consumers?

How do you safely evolve a contract used by many services — prefer additive changes with a compatibility window (new fields optional, deprecate-before-delete, provider contract tests), watch for semantic (not just structural) breaks, and treat a Kafka event as a durable integration contract (schema evolution + backward compatibility for replay) rather than publishing internal JPA entities/DTOs directly?

What is contract-first (spec-first) API development — write the OpenAPI spec as the single source of truth, generate the controller interfaces / client SDKs from it (e.g. `openapi-generator`), and diff the spec in CI to catch breaking changes before any code is written — and how does it differ from code-first (where the contract is implicit in the controllers and can change by accident)?

What is the Circuit Breaker pattern, how does Resilience4j implement it, how does it differ from Retry, and what is the default aspect-order gotcha (Retry wrapping CircuitBreaker, `CallNotPermittedException`)?
How do you secure a microservices architecture (authentication/authorization, API gateway, TLS, service mesh, secrets management, RBAC)?
What security features have you implemented, and explain a JWT + OAuth2 implementation end-to-end (JwtUtil, filter, security config, login endpoint)?
What is JWT, what information does a JWT token contain (header/payload/signature), and can you store sensitive information in the payload?
How do you propagate security tokens from an API Gateway to downstream services (forward Authorization header, inject claims, token exchange, mTLS)?
How do you secure sensitive endpoints from brute-force attacks (rate limiting, account lockout, CAPTCHA, MFA, IP blacklisting, monitoring, short-lived tokens)?
How do microservices maintain sessions when jumping between services (stateless JWT in the Authorization header, each service validates)?
What is a service mesh (data plane sidecars + control plane), what features does it provide, and when should you use it?
Explain Master-Slave architecture, its use cases, and what happens if the master or a slave dies.
What is database sharding, what are its types (horizontal/vertical/geographic/hash), and its advantages and disadvantages?

How do you choose a shard key, and what goes wrong with a bad one — why does an uneven key create a HOT SHARD (one node gets disproportionate data/traffic and caps the whole system's scalability), and why must a good shard key both distribute data evenly AND keep common queries localized to a single shard?

How does sharding change queries and transactions — why is a single-shard query cheap while a query needing data from every shard becomes an expensive SCATTER-GATHER, why are cross-shard transactions complex (no single-node ACID), and why do sharded designs try to co-locate related data and minimize operations that need global coordination?

Why does naive `hash(key) % N` sharding make rebalancing painful (changing N remaps most keys), and how does consistent hashing (with virtual nodes) reduce the data movement when shards are added/removed?

(Scenario) How would you scale a key-value store toward ~1M requests/sec — why is "add more servers" insufficient, and what must you actually specify (how data is partitioned across nodes and how a request is routed to the right node, replication for availability, capacity planning, handling traffic SKEW / hot keys, and what happens when a node fails)?
How do you deploy microservices to containers (Dockerfile, docker-compose, Kubernetes deployment, scaling)?
Explain the full flow of a microservices application (client → API Gateway → service discovery → service → DB → inter-service calls → response → logging/tracing).
Explain the Facade design pattern (a simplified interface to a complex subsystem) with use cases.
If the application suddenly becomes very slow, how do you debug it systematically (CPU, memory, DB, external API, thread pool, logs, thread dumps, JVM metrics)?

How would you debug sustained high CPU in a Java service (collect evidence first — CPU metrics, thread dumps, an async/sampling profiler — to find the hot code paths before changing anything), and what are the common causes (tight loops, expensive serialization, lock contention, pathological regex backtracking, and GC pressure)?

(Scenario) Thousands of threads are suddenly created and CPU spikes — why is "add more servers" the wrong first move, and how do you investigate (thread dumps to see what the threads are doing, thread-creation patterns, missing/misconfigured thread pools creating unbounded threads, excessive context switching, blocking operations, and executor configuration) to decide whether the app is spawning unnecessary threads or using a badly sized pool?
How would you design a system like Uber (actors, services, DB design, real-time location, matching engine, scaling, communication, security, monitoring)?

How would you design a URL shortener (short-code generation — counter+base62 vs hashing, collision handling, read-heavy caching, redirect 301 vs 302, custom aliases, analytics, scaling the key space)?

How would you design an end-to-end payment / order system (synchronous vs Kafka flow, where transaction boundaries live, handling payment and inventory failures with Saga + compensation, idempotent order creation to avoid duplicates, monitoring, and scaling)?

(Scenario) A payment flows across several external banking partners and ONE partner goes down mid-transaction after money has already left the sender — how do you guarantee no money is lost and no double-debit on retry? Compose: a per-partner queue + dedicated consumer so one down partner doesn't block the others (bulkhead), a circuit breaker to detect the failure early and reroute/fail fast, and idempotency keyed by transaction id so a replay after recovery returns the stored result instead of charging again. Critically, why is "just use Two-Phase Commit across the banks" usually the WRONG answer for independent external partners, so you use a Saga with compensating transactions + reconciliation + eventual consistency instead?

How would you model a DOUBLE-ENTRY LEDGER in a relational database so accounting correctness is enforced at the DB level — every financial event writes a balanced set of entries whose debits and credits SUM TO ZERO (money is only ever moved, never created/destroyed), entries are APPEND-ONLY/immutable (corrections are new reversing entries, never updates/deletes), and what DB-level constraints enforce it (a per-transaction CHECK/trigger that the entry set nets to zero, a NOT-NULL account+amount+currency, a unique business key for idempotency, and deriving balances by summing immutable entries rather than storing a mutable balance you can corrupt)?

How would you design a TAMPER-EVIDENT audit log (queryable, 1M events/day, 7-year retention) — make each record cryptographically chain to the previous one by storing `hash(current_record + previous_hash)` so any after-the-fact edit or deletion breaks the chain and is detectable, write to append-only/WORM storage, periodically anchor/checkpoint a signed chain head, and tier old data to cheap cold storage with an index for querying — why is a plain append-only table NOT tamper-EVIDENT by itself, and how does the hash chain close that gap?

How would you design an OTP service that survives a login spike (50k RPS onto a 10k/min SMS provider) — the key fix is the "Resend" button re-sends the EXISTING valid OTP instead of generating a new one, plus multi-level rate limiting, queue buffering with TTL/priority to absorb the spike, provider failover, and TOTP/email as provider-independent fallbacks?

Why is multi-level rate limiting (per-user vs per-IP vs per-provider vs global) more effective than a single limiter, and why must per-provider limits use a token bucket per downstream so you can fail over cleanly when one provider's bucket is empty rather than hammering a rate-limited provider?

How would you design a social feed / timeline at scale (e.g. Instagram/Twitter) — fanout-on-write (push a fully denormalized post entry into each follower's precomputed timeline so reads are an O(1) list lookup) vs fanout-on-read (pull + merge at read time), and why do you use a HYBRID (fanout-on-write for normal users, fanout-on-read for celebrities with millions of followers to avoid massive write amplification)?

How would you design a system to send 1 million (or 100M) push notifications without overwhelming your servers — decouple generation from delivery via a queue, scale a worker fleet independently by queue depth, rate-limit to the provider (e.g. Firebase), make processing idempotent (unique notification ID), use provider batch APIs (1 request → N notifications), add retries → DLQ, generate campaign jobs progressively at very large scale, and track delivery through async provider callbacks?

In a large notification system, how do you stop a bulk marketing blast from starving time-critical messages (OTP/security) — isolate priorities on separate topics/pipelines with their own dedicated consumer groups, so the critical pipeline keeps low latency even when the marketing pipeline is saturated or paused?

Why should you abstract each notification provider (FCM/Twilio/SendGrid) behind a `NotificationProvider` interface, and how do you classify provider errors — non-retryable (invalid token/email → mark failed, do not retry) vs retryable (timeout/5xx/429 → exponential backoff + jitter → DLQ) — so retries don't become a retry storm against a struggling provider?
How would you migrate master data from a legacy system to a custom cloud-based solution (API design, cloud storage, ETL migration, DB setup, monitoring, security, CI/CD)?
Design a microservice to handle uploading large files (100MB+) under high concurrency (streaming, presigned URLs, async metadata queue, reactive WebFlux, backpressure/rate limiting).

Why should uploaded files NOT be stored on or streamed through the application server, how does a presigned URL let the client upload/download directly to object storage (S3/GCS) while your API only mints a short-lived signed URL, how do you upload a very large (multi-GB) file (S3 multipart upload in parts), and why must you validate the actual MIME type / magic bytes and enforce size limits rather than trusting the file extension (plus virus-scan untrusted user content)?

Why does a Spring Boot `MultipartFile` upload fail once the file exceeds ~1–10 MB (`MaxUploadSizeExceededException` / `SizeLimitExceededException`), what are the default limits (`spring.servlet.multipart.max-file-size` ≈ 1MB and `max-request-size` ≈ 10MB), how do you raise them (those properties, or a programmatic `MultipartConfigElement`/`MultipartConfigFactory`), and why is simply raising the limit the WRONG answer for truly large uploads — stream the `InputStream` instead of buffering the whole file in memory (to avoid OOM), and prefer direct-to-object-storage (presigned URL) or chunked uploads?
Write Redis-based distributed lock logic for a scheduled task (`setIfAbsent` with TTL).
Implement a simple round-robin load balancer in Java (`AtomicInteger`).

How would you design a real-time chat / messaging system (e.g. WhatsApp/Slack) — why persist the message to the DB BEFORE delivering it, WebSockets (full-duplex) vs long-polling for delivery, guaranteeing per-conversation message ordering, delivery vs read receipts, presence/typing indicators, offline users (queue + push notification), multi-device sync, and how do you scale stateful WebSocket servers (sticky sessions / a shared pub-sub like Redis so a message published on one server reaches a socket on another)?

How would you design a search service (e.g. product/catalog search) — why NOT run full-text search as `LIKE '%...%'` against the primary DB, how a dedicated engine (Elasticsearch/OpenSearch/Solr) uses an inverted index for millisecond retrieval with ranking/relevance, typo tolerance (fuzzy), filtering/sorting/pagination, and how do you keep the search index in sync with the source of truth (asynchronous indexing via events/CDC, accepting eventual consistency)?

How would you design an autocomplete / type-ahead suggestion service (prefix lookups via a trie or an edge-ngram index, ranking suggestions by popularity/recency, debouncing client requests, caching hot prefixes, and bounding latency to a few ms)?

How would you design a real-time COLLABORATIVE DOCUMENT editor like Google Docs — the core problem is merging CONCURRENT edits from many users without conflicts, so you need either Operational Transformation (OT: transform each incoming op against concurrent ops so all replicas converge, typically via a central server that orders operations) or CRDTs (Conflict-free Replicated Data Types: structures that merge commutatively so replicas converge WITHOUT a central coordinator) — plus persisting the op log / document snapshots, WebSockets for low-latency bidirectional sync, presence/cursors, offline edit buffering + replay on reconnect, and the trade-off between OT (simpler data, needs a server to order ops) and CRDTs (coordination-free, better for offline/P2P, but larger metadata)?

How would you design a recommendation system — start simple (trending/popular, recent activity, category-based rules) before ML, then collaborative filtering (users who liked X also liked Y) vs content-based filtering (similar item attributes), offline precomputation of recommendations vs real-time ranking, event tracking for feedback, and the cold-start problem for new users/items?

How would you design a video streaming platform (e.g. YouTube/Netflix) — why uploads must be processed ASYNCHRONOUSLY (upload → queue → background worker → transcode with FFmpeg into multiple renditions → generate thumbnails → store → publish), adaptive bitrate streaming (HLS/DASH serving different qualities by bandwidth), serving segments from a CDN/edge rather than origin, object storage for the raw/encoded files, and view/analytics tracking?

Why model an order's status as an explicit STATE MACHINE (Created → Confirmed → Preparing → Picked Up → Delivered, with cancel/refund transitions) rather than a free-text `status` field — how does it prevent invalid transitions (e.g. Delivered → Preparing), and how does it pair with the Saga pattern + idempotent order creation in a food-delivery/order backend?
What is the difference between SOA and microservices (ESB vs lightweight protocols, coarse vs fine-grained, shared vs per-service data, centralized vs decentralized governance)?
What is the Outbox pattern, why does writing to the DB and publishing to Kafka in one method risk inconsistency, and how do the outbox table + CDC (Debezium) guarantee delivery?

What happens if the outbox relay/publisher sends an event to Kafka and then crashes BEFORE marking the outbox row as published — the event can be sent again when the publisher resumes, which is expected in an at-least-once design — and why does this mean downstream consumers MUST be idempotent (they may receive the same event more than once), and how do you prevent the outbox table from growing unboundedly (periodic cleanup of published rows, retention policy)?

Why NOT solve the dual-write problem with a distributed/global transaction across PostgreSQL and Kafka, and what is the key distinction between atomicity (all commit together) and recoverability (durable local transactions + explicit eventual consistency + safe retries + reconciliation) — i.e. which invariants truly need synchronous atomicity?

Compare the major architecture styles — Monolith, Modular Monolith, Microservices, Layered (N-Tier), Microkernel/Plugin, Hexagonal (Ports & Adapters), Space-Based, Peer-to-Peer — and the problem each one actually solves.

What is the Hexagonal (Ports & Adapters) architecture, how does it isolate domain logic from infrastructure (dependency inversion), and why is it a style you layer on top of microservices/monolith rather than an alternative to them?
What is the Microkernel/Plugin architecture (stable core + plugins), and where does it fit (IDEs, CMS, rules engines)?
What is Space-Based architecture (in-memory data grid to remove the DB bottleneck), and when is it justified (extreme bursty load — trading, ticketing)?
What is Peer-to-Peer architecture, and when is it the right fit (decentralization as a hard requirement — blockchain, file sharing, mesh)?
What is the difference between a Load Balancer (L4 vs L7), a Reverse Proxy, and an API Gateway, and why are they complementary rather than alternatives?

What is the difference between a forward proxy and a reverse proxy — a forward proxy sits in front of clients and hides them from the server (egress filtering, corporate/VPN, caching outbound requests), while a reverse proxy sits in front of servers and hides them from clients (TLS termination, load balancing, caching, routing) — and which one is Nginx/an API gateway acting as?
What load-balancing algorithms exist (round robin, least connections, least response time, IP hash / sticky sessions, weighted, consistent hashing), and when do you use each?

Why does putting a load balancer in front of app instances break things when a server stores LOCAL state (a session in App A's memory is invisible when the next request lands on App B) — how do you fix it (externalize session/state to a shared store like Redis, or go fully stateless with JWTs), why does round-robin NOT guarantee equal WORK (a 5ms request vs a multi-second one), and why must health checks verify the instance can actually SERVE (dependency/connection-pool healthy) rather than merely be running?
How do you stop the load balancer itself from being a single point of failure (redundant pairs/failover, health checks, DNS failover)?
What is a "distributed monolith" (services that deploy/fail/scale together via shared libraries, shared DBs, synchronous chains), and how do you avoid it?

What are the common microservices anti-patterns and their fixes — over-splitting (start with a modular monolith), chatty services (BFF/aggregation), the "god gateway" (keep business logic out of the gateway), retry storms/thundering herd (backoff + jitter + circuit breaker + retry budgets), tight coupling via shared libraries (share contracts, not code), and no service ownership?

How do you enforce architectural guardrails as automated tests rather than wiki rules — e.g. ArchUnit rules in CI to forbid synchronous service-to-service calls in a transaction's critical path, forbid dual writes (DB + broker without an outbox), forbid controllers calling repositories directly, and enforce layer/package dependencies — and why does codifying these rules prevent architectural drift across a large team?

How do you estimate how many instances/pods are needed for a target throughput (e.g. 1000 TPS) — concurrency = throughput × avg latency (Little's Law), then size CPU/memory and connection pools accordingly?
How do you do a back-of-envelope capacity estimate in a system-design interview (QPS, storage/day→/year, bandwidth, cache size, and the latency numbers every engineer should know)?

How do you approach a broad "Design X" (e.g. Netflix) question in an interview — decompose by user journeys into independent components, then follow Requirement → Responsibility → Data → Technology (and only introduce Redis/Kafka/CDN/sharding where a real bottleneck justifies it) rather than Technology-first?

When would you choose Redis Sentinel versus Redis Cluster — Sentinel for lightweight data (sessions, OTPs, tokens) needing automatic master failover via quorum, Cluster for large/high-QPS caches needing horizontal scaling (data sharded across 16384 hash slots by `CRC16(key) % 16384`, each master with replicas), and why is the first question "what kind of data is in Redis?"

Why is Redis so fast even though command execution is single-threaded — all data is in-memory (no disk I/O on the hot path), an event-driven non-blocking I/O loop (epoll/kqueue) multiplexes many clients, highly optimized data structures, and critically NO lock contention or context-switching between threads for the data — and what did Redis 6.0 add (I/O threads to parallelize network read/write/parsing while command execution stays single-threaded, preserving the lock-free model)?

How do you design a delayed job scheduler at scale — why NOT poll the DB every second (`SELECT ... WHERE execute_at <= NOW()`), and instead use time bucketing / a Redis sorted set (score = execute-at timestamp) to find due jobs efficiently?

Why separate the scheduler (decides WHEN, atomically claims a job `SCHEDULED → QUEUED`) from workers (decide HOW) via a queue, and how do you handle worker crashes (visibility timeout / lease), retries (backoff + jitter → DLQ), cancellation (final state check), and hot time-buckets (shard by `hash(jobId) % N`)?

How does a system recover when a worker node fails — retry first (many failures are transient), then a coordinator (e.g. ZooKeeper) detects a dead node via missed heartbeats and redistributes its work (Competing Consumers pattern), and long-running jobs resume from a checkpoint instead of restarting?

What are the main caching patterns and when do you use each — Cache-Aside (app checks cache, on miss loads DB then populates cache), Read-Through / Write-Through / Write-Behind — and how does an architecture evolve from in-memory (Caffeine) to a distributed cache (Redis) once there are multiple app instances?

What is refresh-ahead caching (proactively recompute a value in the background shortly before its TTL expires so regularly-accessed keys never miss), and how does probabilistic early recompute spread that refresh load so keys don't all refresh at the same instant?

Why is `ConcurrentHashMap.computeIfAbsent(key, expensiveLambda)` a hot-path trap under high TPS — the mapping function runs WHILE holding the bin's lock, so a slow lambda serializes every thread hashing to that bin into a thundering herd (CPU burned on park/unpark context switching, not computation) — and how do you fix it (decouple read from compute: a `Caffeine` `AsyncLoadingCache` with `refreshAfterWrite` returns the STALE value instantly to all readers while ONE background thread recomputes, so zero readers block)?

How does multi-level caching (L1 local in-memory like Caffeine in front of L2 Redis) absorb a stampede burst — when Redis expires a key, each instance briefly serves it from L1 so only one request per instance reloads — and what is the consistency trade-off (short L1 TTL = less stale, longer L1 TTL = stronger DB protection)?

What is the difference between a CDN and Redis (CDN brings static content closer to users at the edge; Redis brings dynamic data closer to the application), and what is a semantic cache for LLM apps (match on embedding similarity rather than exact keys so paraphrased questions reuse a cached answer)?

What is cache penetration (repeated requests for keys that do NOT exist always miss the cache and hammer the database), and how do you defend against it — caching the negative/empty result with a short TTL, and a Bloom filter (a space-efficient probabilistic set with no false negatives: if it says "not present" the key definitely doesn't exist, so you skip the DB lookup entirely)?

What cache eviction policies exist (LRU, LFU, FIFO, TTL/time-based, random) and how do you choose — e.g. LRU/LFU suits a content feed (keep hot items) but is a poor fit for a session store (evicting an active session logs the user out, so size for expected sessions + use TTL) — and why does a low cache hit rate make a cache a net negative (you pay the extra network hop on every miss and still hit the DB)?

Why can a fallback make a system LESS reliable (it silently shifts load to another dependency, returns stale/incorrect data, or hides an outage from monitoring — e.g. a Redis failure that makes every request fall back to PostgreSQL and overwhelms it), and why must fallback capacity be tested independently of the normal path?

Why can an unbounded queue be more dangerous than rejecting requests (it converts overload into unbounded latency + memory growth while appearing available), and why does explicit load shedding / bounded queues preserve healthy latency for work the system can actually complete?

Why can Kubernetes autoscaling make an incident WORSE when the real bottleneck is downstream (PostgreSQL, Redis, an external API) — adding application replicas adds more concurrent callers, connections, and retries against the constrained resource while CPU metrics look healthier?

Why is cascading failure the most dangerous distributed pattern (a small fault amplified through retries, synchronous chains, shared pools, and autoscaling), and what architectural properties contain it (bounded concurrency, deadlines, retry budgets, load shedding, bulkheads, backpressure, graceful degradation)?

How do you test a microservice's failure behavior as a failure contract (inject dependency latency/timeouts, duplicate delivery, process kills between durable steps, cache loss, broker unavailability) with targeted hypotheses rather than indiscriminate chaos?

(Scenario) A critical service has grown to 300,000 lines of code — would you split it into microservices, and what would you evaluate BEFORE deciding (which modules change together, where ownership is unclear, whether failures in one capability affect unrelated capabilities, and whether improving internal boundaries solves the pain without introducing network communication, distributed tracing, service discovery, and cross-service data consistency)?

(Scenario) PostgreSQL is approaching its write capacity — what would you do BEFORE sharding (establish which resource is actually at its limit — CPU, lock contention, connection pressure, WAL generation, a handful of expensive queries — then examine query/index design, transaction duration, unnecessary writes, batching, connection behavior, data lifecycle, vertical headroom, and workload separation, because sharding changes application development permanently)?

(Scenario) A new architecture cuts average latency by 40% but doubles operational complexity — would you approve it, and what would you need to know (which user/business outcome improves, whether tail latency changes, what the existing latency objective is, what additional failure modes appear, and whether the team can operate those components reliably — architecture should not optimize a metric independently of the value attached to that metric)?

When would you deliberately accept data loss — and why is the answer "when the data is reconstructable or low-value enough that guaranteeing durability would cost more than losing it" (telemetry, derived analytics, temporary caches vs financial transactions, ownership records) — and why must you define the acceptable loss window explicitly rather than treating every byte as equally critical?

(Scenario) Your architecture worked well at 10× the original traffic — why might you still replace it (it may have become expensive to change, ownership fragmented, incident recovery requires too much specialist knowledge, infrastructure costs grew disproportionately, regulatory requirements changed, or a component no longer solves a problem the company actually has) — and why should you evaluate architecture against the constraints the organization has TODAY rather than the ones that justified it years ago?

What separates a senior microservices answer from a staff/principal-level answer — a senior engineer can design boundaries, communication, persistence, consistency, resilience, and observability while reasoning about production failure; a staff engineer additionally considers how those choices affect TEAMS (ownership, on-call, migration cost), PLATFORM cost (is the operational tax justified), incident response (can a new team member debug this at 3 AM), and architecture EVOLUTION over years (can services be merged back, can contracts change safely) — the staff-level question is less "can microservices solve this" and more "should the organization pay the permanent cost of this solution"?

(Scenario) A dependency has 99.9% availability but your API is expected to provide 99.99% — is that possible, and how (not if every successful request requires that dependency synchronously — you must remove the dependency from some critical request paths via caching, replication, async workflows, or degraded functionality) — and why must availability targets be translated into concrete behavior rather than SLA numbers alone?

Why does shared-database access between microservices weaken the independence the architecture diagram suggests (schema changes require coordination, business rules can be bypassed, no clear ownership of state), and what are the alternatives (explicit data ownership, controlled interfaces, replicated views, events, reporting stores)?

Why can retries across multiple layers MULTIPLY rather than add — if layer A retries 3×, layer B retries 3×, and layer C retries 3×, one original request can generate up to 27 downstream attempts — and why is this invisible under healthy conditions but becomes the dominant traffic source under degradation (each layer independently decides to retry, and no layer understands the total attempts the complete request generates)?

Why is the word "transient" one of the most expensive words in backend engineering — a timeout might mean the request never arrived, OR the provider is still processing it, OR it completed and the response was lost, OR the system is overloaded and another request is exactly the wrong thing to send — so "transient" doesn't answer whether retrying is safe, only that someone expects the condition to eventually change?

Why does exponential backoff with jitter NOT rescue a bad retry policy (it controls WHEN another attempt happens but doesn't decide WHETHER another attempt should exist — and who in the call chain should OWN the retry decision), and why must retries be treated as a capacity BUDGET rather than free resilience?

(Scenario) A principal engineer suggests removing retries from a payment service — the error rate goes UP but reliability IMPROVES — why (the system stopped using hidden downstream work to make one metric look healthier; failing some requests earlier preserved enough capacity for the system to continue serving the rest, and the dependency recovered faster because it wasn't being hammered by amplified retry traffic)?

(Scenario) A service is healthy according to every dashboard — CPU, memory, pod count, request rate, aggregate error percentage all look normal — but customers report failures. How do you investigate (question what the dashboards are actually measuring — they may miss one tenant/region/endpoint/workflow/dependency path failing, because infrastructure health ≠ business-operation health) — and why must observability extend beyond infrastructure to customer-visible operations and business-level outcomes (a payment system returning HTTP 200 while failing to complete the intended business operation is not healthy)?

(Scenario) How would you migrate hundreds of millions of rows without taking the service offline — separate schema compatibility, data movement, application cutover, and cleanup rather than treating the migration as one deployment: introduce the new representation while the old app remains functional, deploy code that operates during transition, backfill historical data in bounded batches with throttling/observability/restartability, verify correctness continuously, and move reads/writes only after confidence is high — and why does a migration that works in staging behave very differently when competing with production traffic?

(Scenario) How would you introduce a breaking event-schema change used by 15 consumers — why must you avoid requiring fifteen teams to deploy at the same moment (use a compatibility strategy: additive evolution, a new event version, dual publication during a controlled period, or consumer changes before producer changes), and why is the technical schema only part of the problem (once fifteen teams depend on an event, changing it becomes an organizational migration)?

What is the noisy-neighbor problem (one large tenant/customer consuming shared resources — CPU, DB connections, thread pools, queue capacity — and degrading service for everyone else), and what are the isolation strategies: per-tenant quotas, bounded concurrency per tenant, separate queues/pools, workload isolation, resource budgets, and sometimes dedicated infrastructure — and how do you decide which level of isolation the product requires?

How do you prevent one large customer from hurting everyone else when your system is multi-tenant at the application layer but shares infrastructure — and why is "just add more instances" insufficient when the bottleneck is a shared database, a third-party API quota, or a single Kafka partition?

What is the difference between availability (the system can provide service when requested) and reliability (it continues producing CORRECT behavior over time) — a service returning HTTP 200 while producing incorrect financial state may score 99.99% availability on a dashboard while being operationally disastrous — and why must SLIs measure business correctness, not just reachability?

Why is rollback harder in distributed systems than in a monolith — code rollback is easy only when STATE remains compatible; once a deployment writes data in a new schema, publishes events old consumers cannot interpret, or triggers irreversible external side effects, deploying the previous binary may NOT restore the previous system — and why must rollback be considered while DESIGNING the change, not after production begins failing?

(Scenario) You deploy a new version that writes data in a new format, then discover a bug and need to roll back — why can't you simply deploy the old binary (the old code may not understand the new data), and what is the expand-and-contract principle for safe rollback (ensure old and new versions can coexist throughout the migration)?

How would you replace a legacy service without a big-bang migration — find a boundary where traffic or responsibility can move incrementally (a strangler-fig pattern, a compatibility layer, shadow traffic, parallel validation, or consumer-by-consumer cutover) — and why must the design include how the organization RETURNS to the previous state when the new path misbehaves?

(Principal-level) You designed the system — what evidence would make you change your architecture? If you recommend Redis, explain what would convince you it is unnecessary. If you chose async messaging, explain what would make synchronous communication preferable. If you proposed microservices, identify which assumptions justify the boundaries — and why is an architecture much easier to trust when the engineer who designed it can also describe the conditions under which it becomes the WRONG architecture?

How does a service registry like Netflix Eureka work — each service instance registers itself on startup (heartbeat-based lease), clients query the registry to discover available instances, and stale registrations are evicted after missed heartbeats — and how does Kubernetes-native service discovery (CoreDNS + Service objects) differ from Eureka (no separate registry server, the platform handles it), and when do you still need Eureka (non-Kubernetes environments, multi-cloud, gradual migration)?

What is the Raft consensus algorithm — a protocol for achieving agreement across a cluster of nodes on a shared log, using leader election (candidates request votes, majority wins), log replication (the leader appends entries and replicates to followers, committing when a majority acknowledges), and safety (committed entries are never lost even if the leader changes) — and where is it used in practice (etcd for Kubernetes, Consul for service discovery, Kafka KRaft replacing ZooKeeper for metadata consensus)?

What is Kafka? Topics, partitions, offsets? Consumer groups? Producer acks/idempotence? At-least-once/at-most-once/exactly-once? Dead Letter Topic? Kafka Streams? Schema Registry? Kafka Connect? Spring Kafka (@KafkaListener, KafkaTemplate)?

How do you decide between Kafka, AWS SQS, and RabbitMQ for asynchronous communication — using the mental model Kafka = "something happened" (high-throughput durable event streams, multiple independent consumers, retention + replay), SQS = "a job needs doing" (simple managed queue for background work, buffering spikes), RabbitMQ = "route this message" (exchanges, routing keys, bindings for fine-grained routing)?
Explain the main use cases of Kafka (real-time streaming, log aggregation, event-driven microservices, pub-sub messaging, big-data pipelines, CDC, replication/sync, content delivery).

What is Apache Pulsar and how does it differ architecturally from Kafka — a decoupled design (stateless brokers + Apache BookKeeper for storage + a metadata store) vs Kafka's broker-owns-its-storage model, first-class multi-tenancy via tenant/namespace/topic, built-in geo-replication, and support for BOTH streaming (pub/sub) and queue (competing-consumer) semantics with built-in retry + dead-letter topics — and when would you still prefer Kafka (more mature ecosystem, existing infra, raw throughput)?
What is the difference between a topic, a partition, and an offset in Kafka?
Why do we use partitions (parallelism, scalability, ordering within a partition)?
How does Kafka guarantee message ordering within a partition, and what happens with multiple consumers (one consumer per partition per group)?
What is a consumer group, and how does partition assignment work within and across groups?
How does Kafka balance load across consumers in a group, and what happens on join/failure (rebalancing)?
If three instances of a service run and another service sends a Kafka message, how do you ensure only one instance consumes it (same consumer group)?
What is the role of leader and follower replicas, and what is the in-sync replica set (ISR)?
What is the replication factor in Kafka, and what are its use cases?
What is fault tolerance, and how is it achieved using the replication factor (leader election, ISR, acks)?
What replaced ZooKeeper in Kafka 4.0 (KRaft), and why does it matter?
What are the three delivery semantics (at-most-once, at-least-once, exactly-once), and what causes each?
What is the difference between log retention and log compaction?
What happens if a producer sends a message but no consumers are subscribed (retained per retention policy, not discarded like a queue)?
Why would you use a Schema Registry instead of just sending JSON?

What are the trade-offs between JSON, Avro, and Protobuf for Kafka messages, and how does the Avro/Protobuf serializer work with the Schema Registry (the record carries a magic byte + schema id, not the full schema; the "Unknown magic byte" error means a non-schema-registry record — e.g. old JSON — was read with an Avro deserializer)?

What are the Schema Registry compatibility modes (BACKWARD, FORWARD, FULL, NONE), how do they let producers and consumers deploy independently, and why does adding a new required field break compatibility unless you give it a default (so old data can still be read)?
How do you choose a partition key, and what happens if you choose badly (hot partition)?
What are the producer partitioning strategies (round-robin when no key, hash-of-key for ordering per key, custom `Partitioner`), and how does each affect ordering and load distribution?
What is the difference between the eager and cooperative-sticky rebalance protocols?
What is the difference between an idempotent producer and a transactional producer?
How do idempotent producers help achieve exactly-once semantics, and why does it matter?
How do you handle a poison-pill message that keeps failing (dead letter topic)?

(Scenario) A producer sends a message in an unexpected format that the consumer can't deserialize — how do you keep the consumer resilient (safe deserializer, Dead Letter Queue, Schema Registry validation, retries, Kafka Streams `DeserializationExceptionHandler`)?

How do you implement tiered retries for transient failures using retry topics (main → `retry.1s` → `retry.5s` → `retry.30s` → DLQ, graduating a message to the next topic each time it fails) instead of blocking the main consumer, and why use exponential backoff + jitter (to avoid a thundering-herd retry storm) while classifying transient (retry) vs permanent (straight to DLQ) failures?

Once you've fixed the bug that sent messages to the Dead Letter Queue, how do you reprocess them — the "redrive" flow of moving messages from the DLQ back to the main topic/queue so consumers retry them — and how do you do it safely (inspect/replay/discard tooling, idempotent consumers so replays don't cause duplicate side-effects, avoiding re-poisoning the main topic)?

Is a dead-letter queue ENOUGH to handle message failures — no, a DLQ only prevents certain failures from blocking the main processing path; without monitoring (alert on DLQ depth/growth), root-cause classification (transient vs permanent vs poison), a replay/redrive procedure, and clear ownership of remediation, a DLQ becomes a graveyard where failures accumulate silently — why must you treat a DLQ as an incident-response mechanism, not just a configuration option?
What does consumer lag tell you, and what does it NOT tell you (per-partition vs aggregate)?
How does Kafka handle backpressure, and how does it affect consumer lag and throughput (pull model, manual offset, scaling consumers)?
What is `min.insync.replicas`, and why does it matter alongside `acks=all`?
How do you configure producers/consumers for guaranteed delivery (acks=all, retries, transactions, manual offset commit, DLQ)?
What is the default message size in Kafka (1 MB), and which configs control it (message.max.bytes, max.request.size, fetch.message.max.bytes)?
What parameters must be configured for message flow from producer to broker to consumer?
What happens if a message exceeds the default size (RecordTooLargeException), and how do you support larger messages?
How do you optimize Kafka for high throughput (batch.size, linger.ms, compression, acks, max.in.flight)?

What are the trade-offs between the Kafka compression codecs (`compression.type`) — `gzip` (highest ratio, highest CPU), `snappy` (fast, moderate ratio), `lz4` (very fast, low CPU), and `zstd` (strong ratio AND good speed, often the modern default) — why does producer-side batch compression reduce network and disk usage end-to-end, and why should producer and broker codecs be compatible?
Walk through what happens during exactly-once processing end-to-end (transaction coordinator, commit markers, producer ID/epoch fencing).
How many partitions should a topic have, what are the real constraints, and why can you never decrease partition count?
How do you design multi-datacenter Kafka replication, and what is the tradeoff between active-active and active-passive?
When would you deliberately choose NOT to use Kafka?
What is tiered storage (KIP-405), and what problem does it solve?
How do you secure a Kafka cluster in a regulated environment (mTLS/SASL, ACLs, TLS, encryption at rest, network segmentation)?
What happens if a Kafka broker runs out of disk space?
What happens if a consumer crashes after consuming but before committing the offset, and how do you ensure at-least-once (manual offset commit)?

What do the key consumer configs do — `enable.auto.commit` (auto vs manual offset commit, and why manual + commit-after-processing gives at-least-once), `auto.offset.reset` (`earliest` vs `latest` when there is no committed offset), `max.poll.records` (max records per `poll()`, not a total cap), and `max.poll.interval.ms` (too-slow processing between polls triggers a rebalance)?

(Scenario) The consumer app is running with no errors, but messages sit in the topic unconsumed — how do you diagnose it: (1) the consumer group ALREADY committed those offsets (Kafka doesn't redeliver — reset offsets or use a new group.id), (2) auto.offset.reset=latest on a brand-new group SKIPPED all pre-existing messages (set earliest if you need the backlog), (3) more consumers than partitions so some consumers are IDLE (a partition is owned by exactly one consumer per group), or (4) the group is stuck rebalancing — and which tools confirm it (kafka-consumer-groups --describe to see per-partition CURRENT-OFFSET/LOG-END-OFFSET/LAG and member assignment)?

What is the difference between `session.timeout.ms`, `heartbeat.interval.ms`, and `max.poll.interval.ms` for detecting a dead consumer — the background heartbeat thread sends heartbeats every `heartbeat.interval.ms` and the broker evicts the consumer if none arrive within `session.timeout.ms` (detects a CRASHED/unreachable consumer), whereas `max.poll.interval.ms` bounds the time between successive `poll()` calls and evicts a consumer that is ALIVE but stuck processing a batch too long (detects a STALLED consumer) — and why does a slow message handler trigger a rebalance via `max.poll.interval.ms` even though heartbeats are still flowing?
Write a Kafka Streams app that reads a topic, uppercases values, and writes to another topic.
Write a Kafka consumer that routes failed messages to a dead-letter queue.
A rolling deployment triggers a rebalance for every pod restart — why does it hurt more than expected and how do you fix it?
Increasing a topic's partition count from 6 to 12 — what silently breaks (key-to-partition mapping)?
What happens to a "zombie" producer after a network partition heals (epoch fencing)?
With `min.insync.replicas=1`, `acks=all`, replication factor 3 — where is the actual durability risk?
A compacted topic still shows old records for a key you thought was deleted — why (tombstone retention)?
Does the idempotent producer protect you from application-level duplicate publishes?
Your consumer is structurally slower than your producer indefinitely — what happens, given Kafka has no built-in backpressure?
You need exactly-once across a database write and a Kafka publish — why don't Kafka transactions cover this, and what is the fix (transactional outbox)?

(Scenario) A Kafka topic has a hot partition due to skewed key distribution (e.g. one enterprise customer generates 80% of traffic) — how do you fix it without downtime: increasing partitions helps spread NON-skewed traffic but the same key still maps deterministically to one partition (hash(key) % numPartitions), so the real fix is key bucketing/salting (e.g. key = customerId + "-" + hash(orderId) % 4) to split one logical key across multiple partitions — and what is the consumer-side trade-off (must read from multiple partitions and merge results for that customer)?

(Scenario) A Kafka partition reassignment is triggered for scaling/rebalancing and you observe spikes in consumer lag and latency — explain the five causes: (1) data copying saturates disk I/O and network on source/destination brokers, (2) throttling slows replication but keeps the pipe busy longer, (3) leader movement causes consumers to reconnect (NOT_LEADER_FOR_PARTITION errors + metadata refresh), (4) cold page cache on the new broker forces disk reads instead of memory reads until cache warms, (5) coordination overhead from ISR changes and metadata propagation — and why you should monitor replication throughput, avoid reassignment during peak traffic, and throttle appropriately?

Why does Kafka retention cleanup (deleting expired log segments) cause spikes in disk I/O and temporarily degrade broker performance — deletion of many large segment files triggers metadata-heavy random I/O (inode updates, block deallocation) on top of normal sequential read/write traffic, disrupts the OS page cache (invalidated entries force consumers to read from disk), and runs in bursts (scan, batch delete, sleep, repeat) so monitoring shows periodic I/O spikes — and why is this worse on cloud disks like EBS (storage-layer amplification of delete operations)?

In a compacted topic, when and why does data "disappear" even though compaction retains the latest value per key — (1) a tombstone (null value) marks the key for deletion and after `delete.retention.ms` it's removed completely, (2) if `cleanup.policy=compact,delete` BOTH compaction AND time/size retention apply so even the latest record can expire, (3) messages with null or wrong keys bypass compaction entirely and are subject to retention deletion, (4) aggressive compaction settings (small segment size + frequent cleaner runs) remove old records almost immediately — and why is each of these expected behavior, not a bug?

(Scenario) Multiple independent teams share the same Kafka cluster (multi-tenant) and one team suddenly spikes traffic — how do you prevent the noisy-neighbor problem: (1) hard isolation via separate clusters for critical workloads, (2) topic-level isolation (separate topics per team, not one shared topic), (3) Kafka quotas (produce/consume byte-rate limits per client-id/user to throttle the noisy team without dropping messages), (4) partition-level isolation (key by team so hot traffic is contained to specific partitions), (5) retention isolation (different TTLs per topic), (6) broker-level isolation (assign topic partitions to dedicated broker groups), (7) consumer group isolation (independent groups with their own offsets so a slow consumer doesn't block others)?

(Scenario) Partition leaders are moving frequently (due to rebalances, broker instability, or maintenance) — what is the impact: increased produce/consume latency (clients must refresh metadata and retry on NOT_LEADER_FOR_PARTITION), more errors and retries, consumer lag increases during leader transitions, higher broker load from coordination (metadata updates, ISR changes), and risk to durability if replicas fall out of ISR leaving fewer in-sync copies — and how do you stabilize it (fix the root cause of instability, avoid unnecessary preferred-leader elections, monitor leader count per broker)?

Why can Kafka sustain very high throughput on commodity disks — explain sequential append-only writes vs random I/O, zero-copy transfer (`sendfile`), and reliance on the OS page cache rather than an in-process cache.
How is a partition stored on disk (segment files, offset index), and how does retention/compaction interact with segments?

What is the Kafka controller broker (one elected broker managing partition leader elections and broker join/leave), and how does leader election from the ISR (in-sync replicas) keep a partition available when its leader broker fails?

What is the difference between batch processing (bounded data processed in large scheduled chunks — high throughput, high latency) and stream processing (unbounded data processed continuously as it arrives — low latency), and when do you choose each?

What does Spring Kafka add over the raw Kafka client — `KafkaTemplate` (a thread-safe producer wrapper, `send(topic, key, value)` returning a `CompletableFuture`) for publishing, and `@KafkaListener` + listener containers for consuming — and how does the `ConcurrentKafkaListenerContainerFactory` `concurrency` setting map listener threads to partitions (one consumer thread per partition, capped by partition count)?

What are the Spring Kafka `AckMode`s — `RECORD` (commit after each record), `BATCH` (commit after the whole `poll()` batch, the default), `TIME`, `COUNT`, `COUNT_TIME`, and `MANUAL`/`MANUAL_IMMEDIATE` (you call `Acknowledgment.acknowledge()`) — when do you use manual acknowledgment, and why does commit-after-processing give at-least-once semantics?

How do you consume JSON in Spring Kafka (configure `JsonDeserializer` / `spring.kafka.consumer.value-deserializer` with trusted packages), what is the default deserializer, and how do you dynamically pause/resume a listener (`KafkaListenerEndpointRegistry` → `MessageListenerContainer.pause()/resume()`, e.g. to stop consuming while the DB is down)?

How do you handle deserialization failures so one bad payload doesn't block the partition — wrap the deserializer in `ErrorHandlingDeserializer` (so a failed record becomes a recoverable error, not an infinite poison-pill loop) — and what does `DefaultErrorHandler` do (retry with a configurable `BackOff`, classify retryable vs non-retryable exceptions, and send exhausted records to a Dead Letter Topic via `DeadLetterPublishingRecoverer`)?

Explain the CAP theorem (Consistency, Availability, Partition tolerance), why the real choice is CP vs AP, and how it shapes microservices data design (most favor AP/eventual consistency).

Why is "pick consistency OR availability" an oversimplification, and why should the consistency decision START from the business INVARIANT — ask "what must never happen" (e.g. "available balance must never go negative" or "the last item must not be sold twice") demands strong consistency, while "a feed/profile picture can lag a few seconds" permits availability/latency/eventual consistency — so that requirements drive the technology rather than choosing Cassandra-vs-PostgreSQL first?
Explain the ACID properties (Atomicity, Consistency, Isolation, Durability) and transaction isolation levels.

What is the PACELC theorem and how does it extend CAP — during a network Partition choose Availability or Consistency (same as CAP), but Else (when the system is running normally with no partition) you still face a trade-off between Latency and Consistency — and why does this matter (CAP only talks about failure mode, but most of the time the system is healthy and the real daily trade-off is "do I wait for all replicas to ack (consistent but slower) or return after one ack (fast but possibly stale)") — e.g. DynamoDB is PA/EL (available during partition, low-latency normally), PostgreSQL synchronous replication is PC/EC (consistent always, at the cost of latency)?

How do you change a schema on a large production table without downtime using the expand-and-contract pattern (add nullable column → dual-write from the app → backfill in batches → switch reads/add constraints → drop the old column later), and why is a single `ALTER TABLE ... NOT NULL DEFAULT` on a huge table dangerous (table rewrite + long lock)?

Why build an index with `CREATE INDEX CONCURRENTLY` on a busy table, and why should you manage every schema change through versioned migrations (Flyway/Liquibase) instead of `hibernate.ddl-auto=update` in production?

Why do SQL JOINs become prohibitively expensive at very large scale (data sharded across nodes → cross-shard scatter-gather, deep index trees + disk reads per level, large intermediate result sets over the network, and per-user results that cannot be cached), and why does normalized design optimize for write correctness rather than read speed?

What is denormalization as a read-optimization strategy (store data in the shape it is queried, embed related data, keep pre-computed counters updated on each write, use materialized views refreshed in the background) — accepting write amplification and controlled redundancy for fast reads — and what is the guiding rule ("normalize for writes, denormalize for reads")?

What is an application-layer JOIN (fetch each piece by primary key — often from different stores like Redis/Cassandra/PostgreSQL — and assemble in code) versus a database JOIN, and why are point lookups by PK fast and independently cacheable where a multi-table JOIN at scale is not?

What is a SQL transaction (`BEGIN`/`START TRANSACTION` → DML → `COMMIT` or `ROLLBACK`), what does autocommit mode mean (each statement is its own implicit transaction — the default in MySQL/PostgreSQL), and why must you explicitly begin a transaction when multiple statements must succeed or fail together?

What is a savepoint (`SAVEPOINT sp1` → work → `ROLLBACK TO sp1` to undo only the work after the savepoint while keeping the rest of the transaction), and when do you use it (partial retry within a larger transaction, batch processing where one record fails but you don't want to discard the whole batch)?

What does `EXPLAIN` (PostgreSQL/MySQL) show (the query plan the optimizer CHOSE — access method, join order, index usage, estimated rows/cost), how does `EXPLAIN ANALYZE` differ (it RUNS the query and shows ACTUAL rows/time alongside estimates), and why is the first thing you look for a sequential/full-table scan on a large table?

How do you read a plan for common issues — a Seq Scan where an Index Scan was expected (missing index, non-sargable predicate, low selectivity), a Nested Loop with a huge outer table (consider Hash Join), Sort with high cost (missing index for ORDER BY), and vastly different estimated vs actual rows (stale statistics → `ANALYZE` the table)?

What are temporary tables (`CREATE TEMPORARY TABLE`, session-scoped, auto-dropped), when do you use them (staging intermediate results in complex multi-step queries or ETL), and how do they differ from CTEs — a CTE is a named subquery scoped to one statement and usually inlined by the optimizer, while a temp table persists across statements in the session?

Why does a CTE sometimes perform worse than expected (PostgreSQL pre-12 materialized all CTEs as an optimization fence; modern versions may inline them), and when do you force materialization (`MATERIALIZED` / `NOT MATERIALIZED` hints)?

What is an UPSERT (insert-or-update in one atomic statement) — `INSERT ... ON CONFLICT DO UPDATE` (PostgreSQL), `INSERT ... ON DUPLICATE KEY UPDATE` (MySQL), or the SQL-standard `MERGE` — and why is it safer than a separate SELECT-then-INSERT/UPDATE (race condition under concurrency)?

When do you use `MERGE` vs `INSERT ... ON CONFLICT` (MERGE supports matched/not-matched/delete branches for complex ETL; ON CONFLICT is simpler for single-row upserts), and what is the gotcha with upsert + auto-increment (sequence gaps on conflict)?

What is a database sequence (`CREATE SEQUENCE`, `nextval`), how does it differ from an identity/auto-increment column (a sequence is independent of a table — reusable, multi-table, gapless optional; identity is table-bound), and why do sequences have gaps (caching, rollbacks) which is normal and expected?

What is a `CHECK` constraint (`CHECK (salary > 0)`, `CHECK (status IN ('ACTIVE','INACTIVE'))`), when does the DB reject the row (on INSERT or UPDATE that violates), and why is a DB-level CHECK safer than app-only validation (multiple apps, direct SQL, race conditions)?

What are the subquery types — scalar subquery (returns one value, usable in SELECT/WHERE), row subquery (returns one row), table subquery / inline view (returns a result set, used in FROM), and correlated (references outer query) — and give an example of each?

What is the difference between synchronous replication (primary waits for replica to confirm write — strong consistency, higher latency) and asynchronous replication (primary doesn't wait — lower latency, risk of data loss on failover)?
