Explain the Circuit Breaker pattern states (Closed/Open/Half-Open), how you tune thresholds/timeouts/reset-time, whether the breaker can be a single point of failure, how to prevent cascading failures across chained breakers, pitfalls in async/Kafka systems, the fallback-depends-on-failing-service trap, adaptive breakers, and when a breaker is harmful.

Explain the Saga pattern in depth — local transactions + compensations, choreography vs orchestration, idempotent compensations, double-compensation problem, Saga vs 2PC, orchestrator bottleneck, non-reversible side effects, stuck sagas, and long-running consistency.
Explain Inversion of Control (IoC), how Spring implements it, Dependency Injection vs Dependency Lookup, and the three DI types (constructor, setter, field) with pros/cons.
Explain each SOLID principle with violations and fixes, how SRP and DIP can clash during refactoring, and whether SOLID can lead to over-engineering.
What is the DRY ("Don't Repeat Yourself") principle, how do you follow it, and how should it be applied carefully in microservices?

What are the KISS ("Keep It Simple, Stupid") and YAGNI ("You Aren't Gonna Need It") principles — KISS says prefer the simplest solution that works (avoid unnecessary abstraction, over-engineering, or clever code), YAGNI says don't build features or abstractions until they are actually needed (premature generalization wastes effort and adds complexity) — and how do you balance them against DRY (DRY can lead to premature abstraction if you extract a shared module for two things that only look similar today), and what are real examples of YAGNI violations (building a plugin architecture for a service that will only ever have one implementation, adding a message broker when direct REST calls suffice)?
How do you create an immutable class in Java (final class, private final fields, no setters, defensive copies)?
Explain time complexity and space complexity, with common Big-O examples.
For the Prototype pattern, what is the shallow-clone trap, and why is a copy constructor often preferred over `Cloneable` (Bloch's criticism)?
How does Java I/O (`DataInputStream` wrapping `BufferedInputStream` wrapping `GZIPInputStream`...) exemplify the Decorator pattern, and how does it avoid subclass explosion?
Explain the Proxy pattern types (Virtual/lazy, Protection/access-control, Caching, Dynamic/JDK, Remote) and how Spring AOP uses dynamic proxies.
What is the difference between the Facade pattern (new simple interface over complex subsystems) and the Adapter pattern (make one incompatible interface match another)?

How do you approach a low-level design question (e.g. design a Parking Lot, Car Rental, or Elevator system) — identify actors, extract core entities (the nouns), assign single responsibilities, define relationships and interfaces, and apply patterns only where they solve a real problem?

In LLD, how do you model state and behavior cleanly (enums + guarded state transitions vs the full State pattern), when do you use inheritance vs composition for type variants (e.g. vehicle types), and why keep orchestration in a thin service while entities own their own state transitions?

Why is "don't over-engineer" a core LLD skill (avoid forcing patterns, avoid a God class, start simple and refactor), and how do you answer the common follow-up "how would you extend this?" using the Open/Closed Principle (add a new class, not modify existing code)?
What is an anonymous class, when do you use it, what are its restrictions (no constructor, no static members, single base type), and how does it compare to lambdas?
Can an anonymous class extend a class and implement an interface simultaneously?
What does `this` refer to inside an anonymous class, and how do you reference the enclosing instance?
Can an anonymous class access effectively-final local variables, and why the restriction?
What are hidden classes (JEP 371), why were they introduced, how are they created (`defineHiddenClass`), and how do they replace `Unsafe.defineAnonymousClass()`?
How do `ClassOption.WEAK` vs `STRONG` affect hidden-class garbage collection, and what does `NESTMATE` enable?
How do hidden classes compare to dynamically generated `Proxy` classes, and how do they behave under JPMS module restrictions?
What is a sealed class/interface, what are the `permits` rules, and what must permitted subclasses be (`final`/`sealed`/`non-sealed`)?
Can a sealed class permit a subclass in a different package (module vs non-module rules)?
Is listing all permitted subclasses optional if they're in the same file?
Can a sealed class be abstract, and what is the impact on inheritance?
How does sealing improve `instanceof` checks and exhaustive `switch` pattern matching?
Can a sealed class permit itself?
What happens if a permitted subclass has no `final`/`sealed`/`non-sealed` modifier?
Can you serialize/deserialize a sealed hierarchy with Jackson/Gson, and what are the caveats?
How do sealed classes help implement algebraic data types (ADTs)?
If a sealed interface has a `non-sealed` implementor, can an unlisted class extend it?
Can you discover all subclasses of a sealed class at runtime (`getPermittedSubclasses()`)?
Can a sealed class or interface be local or anonymous, and why not?
How are sealed classes and records complementary in Java's pattern-matching vision?
Can you break the sealed contract via reflection or bytecode manipulation?
How does sealing interact with generics and wildcards?
What is Java Vert.x (reactive, event-driven, non-blocking), its features, advantages, and disadvantages?
Can you run batch jobs in Vert.x (setPeriodic, worker verticles/executeBlocking, Quartz cron)?

What is RSocket (reactive binary protocol), its four interaction models (request-response, fire-and-forget, request-stream, channel), features, advantages/disadvantages, and comparison vs WebSockets/gRPC?
How do you implement RSocket error handling, and what happens on client/server disconnect (onErrorResume, retryWhen, keep-alive, resumption)?
Explain backpressure in RSocket and how it differs from HTTP/2 (request(n) demand-based flow control at the application level).
How do you scale an RSocket service in Kubernetes (sticky/consistent-hash LB, client-side LB, HPA on connections, resumable sessions, keep-alive tuning)?
How does RSocket handle retries on failure (client retries, resumable sessions, circuit breakers)?
Can RSocket work in a serverless environment (stateless, cold starts, timeouts; API Gateway WebSocket proxy, always-on server + serverless clients)?
What is gRPC (HTTP/2 + Protocol Buffers RPC), its advantages/disadvantages, use cases, and comparison with REST?
Why does gRPC rely on HTTP/2 instead of HTTP/1.1, and what breaks with HTTP/1.1 (no multiplexing/streaming/binary)?
How does gRPC handle network failures differently from REST (deadlines, retries, circuit breaking), and how do you improve reliability?
How do you add distributed tracing to a gRPC microservice (client/server interceptors injecting/extracting trace context, Jaeger/Zipkin/OpenTelemetry)?
Can gRPC be used in a serverless environment (AWS Lambda), and what are the limitations (cold starts, no connection pooling, no streaming, API Gateway only supports gRPC-Web)?
How do you version gRPC without breaking existing clients (don't change field numbers, use optional fields, add new fields/methods/services, avoid removing/retyping)?
How do you add gRPC-web browser support (Envoy proxy translating HTTP/1.1 ↔ HTTP/2)?
How do you configure mTLS, a JWT auth interceptor, deadlines, compression, and keep-alive for gRPC in Spring Boot?
Implement a gRPC logging interceptor, a rate-limiter interceptor, and a bidirectional streaming service (live stock prices).

What is a `.proto` file and how does gRPC code generation work — you define services (RPC methods) and messages (request/response types with numbered fields) in a `.proto` file, then the `protoc` compiler generates language-specific client stubs and server base classes (Java, Go, Python, etc.) so both sides share a strict, typed contract — and why is this "contract-first" approach stronger than OpenAPI/Swagger (compile-time enforcement, no runtime deserialization surprises)?

What are gRPC status codes — gRPC uses its own set of status codes (not HTTP status codes) such as `OK` (0), `CANCELLED` (1), `INVALID_ARGUMENT` (3), `NOT_FOUND` (5), `ALREADY_EXISTS` (6), `PERMISSION_DENIED` (7), `DEADLINE_EXCEEDED` (4), `UNAVAILABLE` (14), `INTERNAL` (13), and `UNIMPLEMENTED` (12) — how do they map to HTTP codes in gRPC-Web/REST gateways, and how do you return rich error details (Google's `google.rpc.Status` with `ErrorInfo`/`BadRequest` detail messages)?

How do you implement a gRPC service in Spring Boot — add the `grpc-spring-boot-starter` dependency and the protobuf Maven/Gradle plugin, define your `.proto` file, run code generation, annotate the server implementation with `@GrpcService` (extends the generated `ImplBase`), and inject a client stub with `@GrpcClient("service-name")` — and how does service discovery and health checking integrate (gRPC health checking protocol, Kubernetes gRPC probes, Eureka/Consul)?

How does gRPC load balancing work — why does a standard L4 (TCP) load balancer fail for gRPC (HTTP/2 multiplexes all requests over ONE long-lived connection, so the LB sends all traffic to one backend) — and what are the fixes: an L7 (application-layer) load balancer that inspects HTTP/2 frames (Envoy, Istio, AWS ALB with gRPC support), or client-side load balancing where the client discovers backends (via DNS, service registry, or xDS) and distributes calls itself (`round_robin` / `pick_first` policies in the gRPC channel)?
Design an LFU cache with O(1) get/put, and extend it with time-based frequency decay and TTL.

What are the different `OutOfMemoryError` types (Java heap space, GC overhead limit exceeded, Metaspace, Direct buffer memory, unable to create native thread, Compressed class space), and what does each indicate?

What causes memory leaks in Java despite GC (static collections, unclosed resources, ThreadLocal in pools, unremoved listeners, unbounded caches, inner class holding outer reference), and how do you diagnose one end-to-end (jstat → GC log → heap dump → MAT leak suspects → reference chain)?

(Scenario) A service's RSS memory grows steadily but heap dumps and GC logs look CLEAN — how do you investigate an OFF-HEAP leak (it's not on the Java heap, so MAP/heap-dump tools won't show it): check direct/native memory with Native Memory Tracking (`-XX:NativeMemoryTracking`, `jcmd VM.native_memory`), leaked `DirectByteBuffer`s / Netty pooled buffers (missing release), unclosed native resources (JNI, mmap, zip/deflate), thread-stack growth, and Metaspace/classloader leaks — and how do `-XX:MaxDirectMemorySize` and tools like `pmap`/async-profiler help?

What is type erasure in generics, and what does it make impossible (`new T()`, `instanceof List<String>`, generic arrays, overload by generic type), plus the PECS rule (`? extends` producer, `? super` consumer)?
What are Records (Java 16), what does the compiler generate, can you add validation (compact constructor), and what are their constraints (implicitly final, no class extension)?
What are Record Patterns and pattern matching for `switch` (Java 21), and how do they enable exhaustive, type-safe deconstruction of sealed hierarchies (algebraic data types)?
What are Sequenced Collections (Java 21 — `SequencedCollection`/`SequencedSet`/`SequencedMap`, getFirst/getLast/reversed), and what gap did they fill?
How does virtual-thread pinning happen (blocking I/O inside a `synchronized` block pins the carrier thread), and why replace `synchronized` with `ReentrantLock` in virtual-thread-heavy code?
What are Scoped Values (JEP 506, Java 25), and how are they a safer/faster alternative to `ThreadLocal` for virtual-thread workloads?
What is Structured Concurrency / `StructuredTaskScope` (ShutdownOnFailure vs ShutdownOnSuccess), and how does it eliminate orphaned tasks and simplify cancellation?
What is the Java Platform Module System (JPMS, Java 9), what directives does `module-info.java` use (requires/exports/opens/provides/uses), and when is adopting it worth the friction?
What did Java 10 `var` add (local variable type inference), and what are its limitations (locals only, no null, readability trade-off)?

When should you use `var` versus an explicit type — good for obvious initializers (complex generics, stream pipelines, `new HashMap<String,Integer>()` diamond), but avoid it when it hides information (primitives like `int`/`long`/`double`, unclear method-return types, or where a later return-type change would silently compile) — and where is `var` not even allowed (fields, method parameters, return types, lambda parameters without a target type)?

What is off-heap memory (`ByteBuffer.allocateDirect`, Foreign Function & Memory API / Arena in Java 22+), when do you use it (large caches, network I/O, IPC, native integration), and what are the risks?

What are memory-mapped files (`FileChannel.map` → `MappedByteBuffer`), how do they map a file region into memory for OS-paged, zero-copy access, and when are they useful (very large files, high-throughput I/O, inter-process shared memory)?

What are the ways to read a very large text file in Java and their trade-offs — `Scanner` is slow (avoid for big files); `BufferedReader.readLine()` is the simple memory-friendly baseline; `Files.lines(path)` gives a lazy, streaming `Stream<String>` (must be closed — it holds a file handle); low-level `FileChannel` + `ByteBuffer` or a `MappedByteBuffer` (memory-mapped) are fastest for huge files but require manual byte→text handling — and what is the ONE rule that matters most regardless of API (STREAM/process line-by-line or in bounded chunks, never load the whole file into a `List`/`String` in memory, or you risk an `OutOfMemoryError`)?

What are the major OpenJDK projects and what does each change — Loom (virtual threads + structured concurrency), Valhalla (value/primitive classes to flatten objects and kill boxing overhead), Panama (Foreign Function & Memory API + Vector API for native interop and SIMD), Amber (incremental language features: records, sealed types, pattern matching, text blocks), and Leyden (faster startup via AOT/CDS)?

What is Project Skara — the OpenJDK project that migrated the JDK source code from Mercurial to Git and built tooling (bots, CLI tools, and GitHub/GitLab integrations) to modernize OpenJDK's code review and contribution workflow — and why does it matter for contributors (lower barrier to entry, familiar PR-based workflow, faster review cycles)?

How do the major OpenJDK projects work TOGETHER as a coherent platform evolution — Loom (virtual threads) makes blocking I/O cheap so you don't need reactive frameworks, Valhalla (value types) eliminates boxing overhead so primitives work with generics and collections naturally, Panama (FFI + Vector API) replaces JNI for native interop and enables SIMD parallelism, Amber (records, sealed types, pattern matching) makes the language more expressive with less boilerplate, and Leyden (AOT/CDS) makes startup fast for cloud/serverless — and why does a Java developer benefit from understanding the roadmap as a whole (features compound: e.g. Valhalla value types + Loom virtual threads + Panama vectors together enable high-performance, simple, native-interop code that was impossible before)?
What is GraalVM Native Image, how does it change the memory/startup model (AOT, SubstrateVM, Serial GC default, closed-world assumption, reflection hints), and when do you use it vs the JVM?
How does the Foreign Memory API's `Arena` provide explicit, bounds-checked off-heap lifetime management vs GC-dependent DirectByteBuffer cleanup?

How does Java classloading work (Bootstrap → Platform → Application loaders, delegation model), and can two classes with the same fully-qualified name coexist in one JVM (yes — if loaded by different classloaders, as in app servers/plugins)?
How does `ServiceLoader` (the Java SPI mechanism) discover implementations (`META-INF/services` files, lazy loading via the context classloader)?
Why does reflection hurt performance (bypasses many JIT optimizations, incurs access/security checks) yet remain essential for frameworks, and how is it constrained under JPMS strong encapsulation?

How are lambda expressions implemented at the bytecode level (`invokedynamic` + a runtime-generated function object via `LambdaMetafactory`), and why is that cheaper than an anonymous-class instance per lambda?

What are Method Handles (`java.lang.invoke.MethodHandle`) — a strongly typed, directly executable reference to a method, constructor, or field that the JVM can optimize like a direct call — how do you obtain one (`MethodHandles.Lookup` + `findVirtual`/`findStatic`/`findConstructor` with a `MethodType`), how do they differ from reflection (type-safe at creation, faster invocation, access-checked once at lookup not per call, no autoboxing of primitives), and where are they used (the JVM uses them internally for `invokedynamic`/lambda, and frameworks use them for high-performance dynamic dispatch, JSON serialization, and ORM field access)?

What is a Java Agent (`java.lang.instrument`, the `-javaagent` flag, the `premain`/`agentmain` hooks + `ClassFileTransformer`), how does it instrument or rewrite class bytecode at load time (typically via ASM/ByteBuddy/Javassist), and what real tools are built on it (APM like New Relic/Dynatrace, JaCoCo code coverage, OpenTelemetry auto-instrumentation, JRebel hot-reload)?

What is the STAR method, and how do you use it to answer behavioral interview questions as a Java developer — for example, "tell me about yourself", "describe a challenging project", "how do you handle disagreements", and "tell me about a time you failed"?

Design a payment gateway for a bank. Explain the end-to-end architecture, how you guarantee a payment is processed exactly once, how you keep money consistent across services, and how you make the system resilient and observable at scale.

Explain how you secure a banking REST API using OAuth2 and JWT — the token flow, signature validation, access versus refresh tokens — and how you defend against the OWASP top risks such as SQL injection, XSS, CSRF, IDOR, and broken authentication.

Explain the JVM internals — the memory areas (heap, stack, metaspace, code cache), how garbage collection works, what the JIT compiler does, and how you analyze thread dumps, heap dumps, and GC logs when troubleshooting a production Java service.

Solve common coding and DSA interview problems in a finance context — sliding window, two pointers, HashMap lookup, dynamic programming, and tree and graph traversal — and explain the pattern and complexity of each.
Demonstrate practical Java 8 Stream API usage on a finance domain model — grouping, counting, partitioning, sorting, aggregation, and joining — and explain how each collector and operation works.
Find the largest element in an array (keep a variable `max`, update it when you find something bigger).
Find the smallest element in an array (keep a variable `min`, update it when you find something smaller).
Count how many times a given number appears in an array (loop + counter).
Check if a given number exists in an array (linear search — loop through and compare each element).
Reverse an array (swap first with last, second with second-last, using two pointers).
Find the average of all elements in an array (sum / length).
Copy one array into another array.
Print even and odd numbers separately from an array (check `num % 2 == 0`).
What is a String in Java — a sequence of characters, immutable (cannot be changed after creation).
Reverse a string (convert to char array, swap from both ends, or use StringBuilder.reverse()).
Check if a string is a palindrome (same forwards and backwards, e.g., "madam") — compare first and last characters moving inward.
Count vowels and consonants in a string (loop through each character, check if a/e/i/o/u).
Check if two strings are anagrams (same letters in different order, e.g., "listen" and "silent") — sort both and compare, or use character frequency count.
Find the first non-repeating character in a string (use a LinkedHashMap to count frequency, then find first with count 1).
What is a linked list — a chain of nodes, each node holds data + a pointer to the next node; unlike array, nodes are NOT stored side by side in memory.
What is the difference between array and linked list — array has fast access by index O(1) but slow insert/delete; linked list has slow access O(n) but fast insert/delete at head O(1).
Traverse a linked list (start from head, follow next pointers until null, print each node's data).
Find the length of a linked list (traverse and count nodes).
What is a stack — a box where you can only add/remove from the TOP (Last In First Out — LIFO), like a stack of plates.
Implement a stack using an array — push (add to top), pop (remove from top), peek (look at top without removing).
What is a queue — a line where you add at the BACK and remove from the FRONT (First In First Out — FIFO), like a queue at a ticket counter.
Implement a queue using an array — enqueue (add at back), dequeue (remove from front).
What is recursion — a function that calls itself; it needs a base case (when to stop) and a recursive case (when to call itself again).
Write a recursive function to calculate factorial of N (base: `fact(0) = 1`, recursive: `fact(n) = n * fact(n-1)`).
Write a recursive function for Fibonacci number (base: `fib(0) = 0, fib(1) = 1`, recursive: `fib(n) = fib(n-1) + fib(n-2)`).
Print numbers 1 to N using recursion (base: if n == 0 return, recursive: print then call with n-1).
What is a HashMap — a data structure that stores key-value pairs; you give a key, it gives you the value very fast in O(1) average time.
Count the frequency of each element in an array using HashMap (loop through array, for each element increment its count in the map).
Find duplicate elements in an array using HashSet (add each element to set; if `add()` returns false, it is a duplicate).
What is a binary tree — each node has at most 2 children (left child and right child); the topmost node is called root.
What is a binary search tree (BST) — a binary tree where left child < parent < right child; this makes searching fast.
Traverse a binary tree — Inorder (Left → Root → Right gives sorted order in BST), Preorder (Root → Left → Right), Postorder (Left → Right → Root).
What is a graph — a collection of nodes (vertices) connected by edges; can be directed (one-way arrows) or undirected (two-way connections).
What is BFS (Breadth First Search) — visit all neighbors first before going deeper (use a queue); like exploring a maze level by level.
What is DFS (Depth First Search) — go as deep as possible first, then backtrack (use recursion or stack); like exploring one path fully before trying another.
What is sorting — arranging elements in a specific order (ascending or descending).
Implement Bubble Sort — compare adjacent elements, swap if wrong order, repeat until sorted; O(n²) but easy to understand.
Implement Selection Sort — find the smallest element, put it first, then find next smallest, put it second, repeat; O(n²).
Implement Insertion Sort — pick each element and insert it in its correct position in the already sorted part; O(n²) but fast for nearly sorted data.
What is binary search — find an element in a SORTED array by checking the middle; if target is smaller go left, if bigger go right; O(log n) — much faster than linear search.
Implement binary search (iterative) — maintain left and right pointers, calculate mid, compare and narrow down.
What is the difference between linear search O(n) and binary search O(log n) — linear checks every element one by one; binary cuts the search space in half each time but needs sorted data.
FizzBuzz — print numbers 1 to N, but print "Fizz" for multiples of 3, "Buzz" for multiples of 5, "FizzBuzz" for multiples of both.
Check if a number is prime (no factors other than 1 and itself — loop from 2 to sqrt(n)).
Check if a number is palindrome (e.g., 121 → reverse digits → 121 → same → palindrome).
Find the GCD (Greatest Common Divisor) of two numbers using Euclidean algorithm (`gcd(a,b) = gcd(b, a%b)`, base: `gcd(a,0) = a`).
Print all prime numbers up to N (Sieve of Eratosthenes — mark multiples of each prime as not-prime).
Swap two numbers without using a third variable (using XOR: `a = a ^ b; b = a ^ b; a = a ^ b` or using addition: `a = a + b; b = a - b; a = a - b`).
Check if a string contains only digits (loop through each character, check `Character.isDigit()`).
Remove all spaces from a string.
Convert a string to uppercase / lowercase without using built-in methods (add/subtract 32 from ASCII value).
Print a right-angled triangle pattern of stars using nested loops.
Find the power of a number (e.g., 2^10) using recursion (`power(x,n) = x * power(x, n-1)`, base: `power(x,0) = 1`).
Find the largest / smallest element in an array (single pass, O(n)).
Find the second-largest element without sorting (track top two in one pass).
Reverse an array in-place (two-pointer swap from ends).
Check if an array is sorted (compare adjacent elements).
Remove duplicates from a sorted array in-place (slow=insert position, fast=scan).
Move all zeros to the end while preserving order (two-pointer swap).
Rotate an array by K positions (reverse whole → reverse first K → reverse rest).
Find the missing number in 1..N (sum formula or XOR trick).
Contains Duplicate — check using HashSet in O(n).
Two Sum — return indices of pair summing to target (HashMap of complement).
Best Time to Buy and Sell Stock — single pass tracking min price, max profit.
Sort 0s, 1s, 2s in one pass (Dutch National Flag — three pointers).
Max Consecutive Ones — count longest run of 1s.
Product of Array Except Self — prefix × suffix product, no division.
3Sum — sort + fix one + two-pointer scan, skip duplicates.
Container With Most Water — two-pointer from ends, move shorter side.
Trapping Rain Water — two-pointer tracking left-max and right-max.
Maximum Subarray / Kadane's Algorithm — running sum, reset when negative.
Maximum Product Subarray — track running max AND min (negatives flip).
Find Minimum in Rotated Sorted Array — binary search on inflection.
Search in Rotated Sorted Array — binary search checking which half is sorted.
Merge two sorted arrays in-place.
Find all duplicates in an array (index-marking or frequency map).
Encode and Decode Strings — design encode/decode for list of strings.
Median of Two Sorted Arrays — binary search partition, O(log min(m,n)).
Largest number from a list of integers (custom comparator: compare `a+b` vs `b+a`).
Reverse a string without StringBuilder (two-pointer swap on char array).
Check if a string is a palindrome (two-pointer, skip non-alphanumeric).
First non-repeating character (LinkedHashMap).
Valid Anagram — character frequency comparison (26-size array or HashMap).
Group Anagrams — sort each word as key, group by sorted key.
Longest Common Prefix — vertical scan comparing characters.
Longest Substring Without Repeating Characters (sliding window + HashSet).
Longest Repeating Character Replacement — sliding window, `windowSize - maxFreq ≤ K`.
Longest Palindromic Substring — expand-around-center O(n²) or Manacher's O(n).
Palindromic Substrings — count all (expand-around-center).
Minimum Window Substring — sliding window with frequency map.
Valid Parentheses — stack matching pairs.
Longest Valid Parentheses — stack tracking indices.
Valid Parenthesis String with `*` wildcard — greedy min/max open-count range.
Check if two strings are rotations of each other (`s1+s1` contains `s2`).
Explain the Two Pointers technique — opposite-end vs same-direction vs fast/slow variants.
Two Sum on sorted array — left+right pointer, O(1) space.
Remove Duplicates from Sorted Array — slow/fast pointer.
Move Zeroes — two-pointer compaction.
Valid Palindrome — left/right skipping non-alphanumeric.
Container With Most Water — opposite-end, move shorter side.
3Sum — sort + two-pointer for remaining pair.
Trapping Rain Water — two-pointer with left-max/right-max.
Sort Colors (Dutch National Flag) — three pointers for 0s, 1s, 2s.
Explain Sliding Window — fixed-size vs variable-size window, expand right / shrink left.
Maximum Sum Subarray of Size K — fixed-size window, add right, subtract left.
Minimum Size Subarray Sum ≥ target — variable window, shrink when condition met.
Longest Substring Without Repeating Characters — variable window + HashMap.
Longest Repeating Character Replacement — window where `size - maxFreq ≤ K`.
Find All Anagrams in a String — fixed-size window with frequency comparison.
Fruit Into Baskets / Longest with At Most K Distinct — variable window + char count.
Minimum Window Substring — expand/shrink with frequency map + matched count.
Sliding Window Maximum — monotonic deque maintaining decreasing order.
Max Consecutive Ones III — sliding window allowing at most K zero flips.

Detect a cycle in a linked list (Floyd's slow/fast pointer).
Linked List Cycle II — find the start of the cycle.
Happy Number — detect cycle in digit-sum sequence using fast/slow.
Find the Duplicate Number — Floyd's on index→value mapping.
Reverse a linked list — iterative (prev/curr/next) and recursive.
