Merge K sorted linked lists into one single sorted linked list. You are given an array of K list heads, each list already sorted ascending, and you must return one combined sorted list efficiently.
Given the head of a singly linked list, remove the Nth node counting from the end of the list and return the head. Do it in a single pass.
Given the head of a singly linked list, determine whether the list reads the same forwards and backwards. Do it in O(n) time and O(1) extra space, and ideally restore the list afterwards.
Given a singly linked list L0 to L1 to ... to Ln, reorder it to L0 to Ln to L1 to Ln-1 to L2 to Ln-2 and so on. You may not change node values, only rearrange the nodes themselves.

You are given two non-empty linked lists representing two non-negative integers, with digits stored in reverse order and each node holding a single digit. Add the two numbers and return the sum as a linked list, also in reverse order.

A linked list is given where each node has a next pointer and an additional random pointer that can point to any node in the list or to null. Construct a deep copy of the list such that the copied nodes mirror the next and random structure without referencing any original node.

Given the heads of two singly linked lists, return the node at which the two lists intersect. If they do not intersect, return null. The intersection is by node identity, not by value, and the lists keep their original structure.
Given a sorted array of integers and a target value, return the index of the target if it is present, otherwise return minus one. The algorithm must run in logarithmic time.

Given a sorted array that may contain duplicates and a target value, find the first and last index where the target appears. Return minus one for both if the target is absent. The algorithm must run in logarithmic time.

Given a sorted array of distinct integers and a target value, return the index where the target is found. If it is not found, return the index where it would be inserted to keep the array sorted. Run in logarithmic time.
A sorted ascending array of distinct integers has been rotated at some unknown pivot. Find the minimum element in logarithmic time.
A sorted ascending array of distinct integers is rotated at an unknown pivot. Given a target, return its index or minus one if absent. Run in logarithmic time.

A peak element is one that is strictly greater than its neighbors. Given an array where neighbors differ, return the index of any peak. Assume elements outside the array are negative infinity. Run in logarithmic time.

Koko has piles of bananas and h hours before the guards return. Each hour she eats up to a chosen speed k bananas from one pile. Find the minimum integer speed k such that she can finish all piles within h hours. Run in logarithmic time over the speed.

Given package weights in loading order and D days, find the minimum ship capacity per day so that all packages are shipped within D days. Packages must be shipped in the given order and cannot be split across ships.
Given two sorted arrays, find the median of the combined sorted order of all elements in O(log(min(m, n))) time, without actually merging the arrays.

Given a non-negative integer, compute and return its integer square root, the largest integer whose square does not exceed the input. Do it without using any built-in square root function, in logarithmic time.
Explain the prefix sum technique. How does precomputing cumulative sums let you answer range sum queries in constant time, and when should you use it?
Design a class that, given an immutable integer array, answers multiple queries for the sum of elements between indices i and j inclusive. The constructor may preprocess, and each query must be fast.
Given an integer array and an integer K, count the total number of contiguous subarrays whose elements sum to exactly K. The array may contain negative numbers.
Given a binary array of zeros and ones, find the length of the longest contiguous subarray that contains an equal number of zeros and ones.
Given an integer array, return an array where each position holds the product of all other elements, without using division and in linear time.
Given an unsorted integer array, find the length of the longest run of consecutive integers. The numbers may appear in any order, and the algorithm must run in linear time.
Given an integer array and an integer K, return the K most frequent elements. The answer may be in any order and the algorithm should be better than O(n log n) where possible.
Given a string containing just the characters `(`, `)`, `{`, `}`, `[` and `]`, determine if the input string is valid — brackets must be closed in the correct order by a matching pair.
Design a stack that supports push, pop, top, and retrieving the minimum element, all in constant time.
Implement a first-in-first-out queue using only two stacks. Also discuss implementing a stack using two queues.
Given an arithmetic expression in Reverse Polish (postfix) notation, evaluate it and return the result.
Given two arrays `nums1` (a subset of `nums2`), for each element in `nums1` find the next greater element to its right in `nums2`. If none exists, return -1 for that element.
Given an array of daily temperatures, return an array where each position holds the number of days you must wait until a warmer temperature. If no warmer day exists, put 0.
Given an array of bar heights representing a histogram where each bar has width 1, find the area of the largest rectangle that fits entirely within the histogram.
Given an array and a window size k, return the maximum value in each contiguous window of size k as the window slides from left to right.
Given the root of a binary tree, return its maximum depth, which is the number of nodes along the longest path from the root down to the farthest leaf.
Given the roots of two binary trees, determine whether they are structurally identical and have the same values at every corresponding node.
Given the root of a binary tree, invert it so that the left and right children of every node are swapped, producing a mirror image of the original tree.
Given the root of a binary tree, return its level order traversal, meaning the node values grouped level by level from top to bottom, left to right within each level.
Implement the three depth-first traversals of a binary tree — inorder, preorder, and postorder — both recursively and iteratively using an explicit stack.

Given the root of a binary tree, determine whether it is a valid binary search tree, where every node's value is greater than all values in its left subtree and less than all values in its right subtree.
Given the root of a binary search tree and an integer k, return the kth smallest value in the tree.
Given the root of a binary tree and two nodes, find their lowest common ancestor, which is the deepest node that has both target nodes as descendants.

Given a tree and a non-empty list of employees/nodes (which may contain duplicates), return the deepest node whose subtree contains ALL of them. Deduplicate the targets, then in postorder count target nodes in each subtree (including the root), returning the deepest node containing every distinct target in O(N + K) time and O(N) space. Follow-up: if the tree is fixed but you receive thousands of queries, separate preprocessing cost from per-query cost using an Euler-tour and sparse table for O(1) LCA per pair.
Given the root of a binary tree, return the length of its diameter, which is the number of edges on the longest path between any two nodes, and this path may or may not pass through the root.
Given the root of a binary tree, find the maximum path sum, where a path is any sequence of connected nodes and the path need not pass through the root. Each node's value may be negative.
Given the roots of two binary trees root and subRoot, return true if there is a subtree of root with the same structure and values as subRoot.
Given two arrays representing the preorder and inorder traversal of a binary tree with unique values, reconstruct and return the original tree.
Design an algorithm to serialize a binary tree to a string and deserialize that string back into the identical tree.
Given the root of a binary tree, return the values of the nodes you can see when looking at the tree from the right side, ordered from top to bottom.
Given the root of a binary tree, determine whether it is height-balanced, meaning that for every node the heights of its left and right subtrees differ by at most one.

Path Sum: given a tree and a target, determine if any root-to-leaf path sums to the target. Path Sum III: count the number of downward paths (not necessarily starting at the root or ending at a leaf) whose values sum to the target.
Design and implement a prefix tree (Trie) supporting three operations: insert a word, search whether an exact word exists, and check whether any stored word starts with a given prefix.

Design a data structure that supports adding words and searching words, where the search string may contain the dot character '.' that matches any single letter. Return whether any stored word matches the pattern.

Given an m by n board of characters and a list of words, return all words that can be formed by sequentially adjacent cells (horizontally or vertically neighboring), where each cell is used at most once per word.
Given a dictionary of root words and a sentence, replace every word in the sentence that has a root in the dictionary as a prefix with the shortest such root. Return the resulting sentence.
Given an unsorted array of integers and a value K, return the Kth largest element (by value, not the Kth distinct element).
Given an array of elements and a value K, return the K most frequent elements, in any order.
Given K sorted linked lists, merge them into one sorted linked list and return its head.
Design a data structure that supports adding integers from a stream and returning the median of all values added so far, in logarithmic add time and constant median time.

Design a class that is initialized with a value K and an initial list of numbers, and supports an add operation that inserts a new number and returns the Kth largest element among all numbers seen so far.
Given an array of points on a plane and a value K, return the K points closest to the origin, where distance is Euclidean (the square root of x squared plus y squared).

Given a list of tasks represented by characters and a cooldown value N, where the same task must be separated by at least N intervals, return the minimum number of intervals needed to finish all tasks (idle intervals count).

Given a two-dimensional grid of '1's (land) and '0's (water), count the number of islands, where an island is formed by connecting adjacent land cells horizontally or vertically and is surrounded by water.
Given a reference to a node in a connected undirected graph, return a deep copy of the entire graph, where each node contains a value and a list of its neighbors.

Given a grid of cell heights, water can flow from a cell to a neighbor of equal or lower height. The Pacific borders the top and left edges, the Atlantic the bottom and right. Return all cells from which water can reach both oceans.

Given a grid where each cell is empty, a fresh orange, or a rotten orange, every minute any fresh orange adjacent to a rotten one becomes rotten. Return the minimum minutes until no fresh orange remains, or negative one if impossible.

Given an image as a grid of pixel colors, a starting pixel, and a new color, repaint the starting pixel and all connected pixels of the same original color with the new color, where connectivity is orthogonal. Return the modified image.

Given a begin word, an end word, and a dictionary of equal-length words, return the length of the shortest transformation sequence from begin to end, where each step changes exactly one letter and every intermediate word is in the dictionary, or zero if none exists.
Given a board of 'X' and 'O', capture all regions surrounded by 'X' by flipping every 'O' that is not connected to a border 'O' into 'X'. Border-connected 'O's are safe and stay.
Given a number of courses and a list of prerequisite pairs, return whether it is possible to finish all courses, which is true if and only if the prerequisite graph has no cycle.
Given a number of courses and a list of prerequisite pairs, return any valid ordering in which all courses can be taken, or an empty array if no such ordering exists because of a cycle.
Given n nodes labeled 0 to n minus 1 and a list of undirected edges, determine whether these edges form a valid tree, meaning the graph is fully connected and contains no cycle.
Given n nodes labeled 0 to n minus 1 and a list of undirected edges, return the number of connected components in the graph.
Implement topological sorting of a directed acyclic graph using Kahn's algorithm, which processes nodes in order of their in-degree reaching zero, and detect a cycle if not all nodes can be ordered.
Implement topological sorting of a directed acyclic graph using depth-first search, producing the order by reversing the post-order of the DFS.

Given courses with prerequisites, provide a single approach that both detects whether all courses can be finished (Course Schedule I) and, when possible, returns a valid completion order (Course Schedule II), using topological sorting.
Explain the Union-Find / Disjoint Set data structure. How do find(x) with path compression and union(x,y) by rank achieve near-constant amortized time?
Given n nodes and a list of undirected edges, count the number of connected components using Union-Find.
In a graph that started as a tree with n nodes and had one extra edge added, return the edge that creates a cycle (if multiple, return the last one in input order).
Given a 2D grid of '1' (land) and '0' (water), count the number of islands using Union-Find instead of DFS/BFS.
You start with an all-water grid and add land one cell at a time. After each addition, report the current number of islands. Use Union-Find with path compression and union by size.
Given accounts where each is a name followed by emails, merge accounts that share any email. Return merged accounts with the name and sorted unique emails.
Given an n×n adjacency matrix where isConnected[i][j] = 1 means city i and city j are directly connected, return the number of provinces (connected groups of cities).
Given an array of distinct integers, return all possible subsets (the power set) using backtracking.
Given an array that may contain duplicates, return all unique subsets using backtracking.
Given an array of distinct integers, return all possible orderings (permutations) using backtracking.
Given an array that may contain duplicate integers, return all unique permutations.
Given distinct candidates and a target, return all unique combinations that sum to target. Each candidate may be used an unlimited number of times.
Given candidates that may contain duplicates and a target, return all unique combinations summing to target, where each candidate may be used at most once.
Given a string of digits 2–9, return all letter combinations the number could spell, based on the classic phone keypad mapping.
Given n pairs of parentheses, generate all combinations of well-formed (balanced) parentheses.
Given a string, partition it so that every substring of the partition is a palindrome, and return all possible palindrome partitionings.
Given a 2D board of characters and a word, return true if the word exists in the grid by connecting horizontally or vertically adjacent cells, where each cell is used at most once.
Place n queens on an n×n chessboard so that no two queens attack each other, and return all distinct solutions (or the count).
Write a program to solve a 9×9 Sudoku board by filling empty cells so that every row, column, and 3×3 box contains the digits 1–9 exactly once.
How do you recognize that a problem should be solved with dynamic programming? Explain overlapping subproblems and optimal substructure, and the difference between memoization and tabulation.
You can climb 1 or 2 steps at a time. In how many distinct ways can you reach the top of n stairs?
Given an array of non-negative house values, find the maximum amount you can rob without robbing two adjacent houses.
Given an array of daily prices, find the maximum profit from a single buy and a single later sell. If no profit is possible, return 0.
Find the contiguous subarray with the largest sum and return that sum. Explain Kadane's algorithm.
Given coin denominations and a target amount, return the fewest number of coins needed to make that amount, or -1 if it cannot be made.
Given coin denominations and a target amount, return the total number of distinct combinations that make up that amount (order does not matter). Coins may be reused.
Given two strings, return the length of their longest common subsequence — characters that appear in both in the same relative order but not necessarily contiguously.
Given an array of integers, return the length of the longest strictly increasing subsequence. Aim for O(n log n).
Given two strings, return the minimum number of single-character insertions, deletions, or replacements needed to turn the first string into the second.
Given item weights and values and a knapsack capacity, maximize total value where each item may be taken at most once (0 or 1).
Given an array of positive integers, determine whether it can be split into two subsets with equal sums.
Given a string and a dictionary of words, determine whether the string can be segmented into a space-separated sequence of one or more dictionary words.
A message of digits is encoded where 1 maps to A through 26 maps to Z. Given a digit string, count how many ways it can be decoded.
A robot starts at the top-left of an m by n grid and may move only right or down. Count how many distinct paths reach the bottom-right.
Given an m by n grid of non-negative costs, find a path from top-left to bottom-right that minimizes the sum of costs, moving only right or down.
Given an array where each element is the maximum jump length from that position, determine whether you can reach the last index starting from the first.
Given an array where each element is the maximum jump length, return the minimum number of jumps needed to reach the last index (assume the end is always reachable).
Given a string, return the longest contiguous substring that reads the same forwards and backwards.
Given a string, return the length of the longest subsequence that reads the same forwards and backwards (characters need not be contiguous).
Given an integer array, find the contiguous subarray with the largest product and return that product.
Given two strings, return the length of the longest substring (contiguous) that appears in both.
Given an array of non-negative integers and a target, assign a plus or minus sign to each number so the signed sum equals the target, and count the number of ways.
Given strings s1, s2, and s3, determine whether s3 is formed by interleaving s1 and s2, preserving the left-to-right order of each.
Given strings s and t, count the number of distinct subsequences of s that equal t.
Implement regular expression matching where '.' matches any single character and '*' matches zero or more of the preceding element, over the entire input string.
Implement wildcard pattern matching where '?' matches any single character and '*' matches any sequence of characters including the empty sequence.
Given balloons with values, bursting balloon i yields nums[left]·nums[i]·nums[right] where left and right are the adjacent unburst balloons. Maximize the total coins from bursting all balloons.
Given the dimensions of a chain of matrices, find the minimum number of scalar multiplications needed to compute the product, choosing the best parenthesization.
Given a string of only '(' and ')', return the length of the longest substring that is a valid (well-formed) parentheses sequence.
A robot moves only right or down on an m by n grid where some cells are blocked (marked 1). Count distinct paths from top-left to bottom-right; blocked cells cannot be entered.
Explain Cyclic Sort. Given an array containing numbers in the range [1, n] (or [0, n-1]), sort it in O(n) time and O(1) extra space by swapping each number to its correct index.
Given a string containing the bracket characters round, square, and curly, determine whether every opening bracket is closed by the matching type in the correct order, using a stack.
Given an array containing n distinct numbers taken from the range [0, n], find the one number that is missing. Solve using cyclic sort in O(n) time and O(1) space.
Design a stack that supports push, pop, top, and retrieving the minimum element, with every operation running in constant time.

Given an array of n integers where each value is in the range [1, n] and some values appear twice while others are missing, return all the numbers in [1, n] that do not appear. Use O(n) time and O(1) extra space (output array does not count).
Given an arithmetic expression in Reverse Polish Notation (postfix), where operators follow their operands, evaluate it and return the result using a stack.

Given an array of n+1 integers where each value is in the range [1, n], exactly one value is repeated (possibly multiple times). Find the duplicate without modifying the array ideally, in O(n) time and O(1) space. Explain both cyclic sort and Floyd's approaches.
Implement a first-in-first-out queue using only two last-in-first-out stacks, supporting enqueue and dequeue, and analyse the amortised cost.
Given an unsorted integer array, find the smallest missing positive integer in O(n) time and O(1) extra space. The array may contain negatives, zeros, and duplicates.
Design a fixed-capacity cache that evicts the least recently used entry when full, supporting get and put in constant time.
Given a non-empty array where every element appears twice except for one element that appears once, find that single element in O(n) time and O(1) space.
Given an array of numbers and a value k, find the kth largest element efficiently using a priority queue (heap).
Write a function that counts the number of set bits (bits equal to 1) in the binary representation of an integer, ideally in O(number of set bits) time. Explain the n & (n-1) trick.
Given k sorted lists, merge them into one sorted list efficiently using a priority queue (heap).
Given an integer n, return an array of length n+1 where the entry at index i is the number of set bits in i. Solve in O(n) time using dynamic programming.
Given an array of elements, return the k elements that appear most frequently, using a hash map to count and a heap to select.
Reverse the bits of a given 32-bit unsigned integer. For example, the binary representation read from the most significant bit becomes the least significant bit and vice versa.
Implement a trie supporting inserting a word, searching for a complete word, and checking whether any word starts with a given prefix.
Given an array containing n distinct numbers taken from the range [0, n], find the missing number using the XOR technique. Compare it with the sum approach.
Implement the union-find (disjoint set) data structure supporting find and union, with path compression and union by rank, and explain its near-constant time complexity.
Determine whether a given integer is a power of two. Solve in O(1) time using a single bitwise expression and explain why it works.
Given a two-dimensional grid of land and water cells, count how many separate islands exist, where an island is land connected horizontally or vertically.
Compute the sum of two integers a and b without using the + or - operators. Explain the bitwise approach using XOR and carry.
Given tasks with prerequisite dependencies, produce a valid order to complete them, or detect that no order exists because of a cycle, using topological sort.
Explain Bubble Sort, Selection Sort, and Insertion Sort. What is the time complexity of each, which are stable, and when would you use each one?
Given a set of distinct elements, generate all possible subsets, also called the power set, using backtracking.
Explain Merge Sort. Why is it O(n log n), why is it stable, and what are its trade-offs compared to Quick Sort?
Given a set of distinct elements, generate all possible orderings (permutations) using backtracking.
Explain Quick Sort. Why is it O(n log n) on average but O(n²) worst case, how do you avoid the worst case, and why is it not stable?
Given a set of distinct positive numbers and a target, find all unique combinations that sum to the target, where each number may be reused unlimited times.
Explain Heap Sort. How does building the heap take O(n), why is the overall sort O(n log n), and when would you choose it over Quick Sort or Merge Sort?
Place n queens on an n-by-n chessboard so that no two queens attack each other, and count or list all valid placements, using backtracking.
Explain Counting Sort and Radix Sort. Why are they O(n+k) rather than O(n log n), when can you use them, and are they stable?
Given a grid of characters and a word, determine whether the word can be formed by a path of orthogonally adjacent cells, where each cell is used at most once.
Explain Dijkstra's shortest path algorithm. Why does it require non-negative edge weights, how does the min-heap version achieve O((V+E) log V), and how do you reconstruct the path?
Given n pairs of parentheses, generate all combinations of well-formed (balanced) parentheses, using backtracking with constraints.
Explain Bellman-Ford. How does it handle negative edge weights, how does it detect a negative cycle, and why is it O(V·E) rather than O((V+E) log V)?
Given a collection of intervals, merge all overlapping intervals and return the non-overlapping intervals that cover the same ranges.

Given a network of n nodes and directed travel times, find how long it takes for a signal sent from a source node k to reach all nodes, or return -1 if some node is unreachable. Solve with Dijkstra's.
Given a set of meetings with start and end times, find the minimum number of rooms needed so that no two overlapping meetings share a room.
Explain the Knuth-Morris-Pratt string matching algorithm. What is the failure (prefix) function, why does it give O(n+m) matching, and how is the table built?
Implement the quick sort algorithm, explain the partition step and pivot choice, and analyse its time complexity.
Explain the Rabin-Karp string matching algorithm. How does the rolling hash work, why is it O(n+m) on average but O(n·m) worst case, and why is it good for multiple-pattern search?
Implement the merge sort algorithm, explain the divide and merge steps, and analyse its time and space complexity and stability.
Compare KMP, Rabin-Karp, and brute-force substring search. When would you pick each one in a real system, considering time complexity, multiple patterns, and worst-case guarantees?
Implement heap sort using a binary heap, explain the heapify and sort-down phases, and analyse its complexity and stability.
Rotate an n by n matrix 90 degrees clockwise in place. Explain why transpose followed by reversing each row works and the time and space complexity.
Determine whether a singly linked list contains a cycle, and find the node where the cycle begins, using Floyd's two-pointer algorithm in constant space.
Given an m by n matrix, return all its elements in spiral order, starting from the top-left and moving right, down, left, up, spiraling inward. Explain the boundary approach and its complexity.
Given a singly linked list, reverse its nodes k at a time and return the modified list, leaving any trailing group of fewer than k nodes in original order.
Search a 2D Matrix — binary search on flattened or top-right elimination.
Set Matrix Zeroes — first row/column as markers.
Word Search — DFS backtracking on grid.
Flood Fill — BFS/DFS from starting cell.
LRU Cache — HashMap + doubly linked list, O(1) get/put.
LFU Cache — HashMap + frequency map + LinkedHashSet.
Min Stack — O(1) push/pop/top/getMin.
RandomizedSet — array + HashMap for O(1) insert/remove/getRandom.
Time-Based Key-Value Store — map of key→sorted(timestamp, value), binary search.
Implement Queue using Stacks / Stack using Queues.

Cache with TTL and Versioned Expiry — implement `put(key, value, ttl, now)` and `get(key, now)` where an entry is valid only while `now < expires_at`; a newer write replaces the old value AND expiry, so an old cleanup event must NOT delete a newer version of the same key (attach a version/sequence to each expiry record and verify it still matches before deleting) — lazy expiry gives O(1) per op; a heap for proactive cleanup adds O(log n) and stale-record management.

Given a sorted array of numbers and a target sum, find a pair of elements whose values add up exactly to the target and return their indices. Solve it with the two-pointer technique. (LeetCode: Two Sum II — Input Array Is Sorted)
Given an array containing only 0s and 1s, rearrange it in place so that all the 0s come first followed by all the 1s, without using any extra array. (GeeksforGeeks: Segregate 0s and 1s)

Given a sorted array (or a sorted linked list), remove the duplicate elements in place so that each element appears only once, and return the new length (or the de-duplicated list). Solve it without allocating a second structure. (LeetCode: Remove Duplicates from Sorted List / Remove Duplicates from Sorted Array)

Given an array sorted in non-decreasing order that may contain negative numbers, return a new array of the squares of each number, also sorted in non-decreasing order. Aim for linear time. (LeetCode: Squares of a Sorted Array)
Given an array of numbers, find all unique triplets that add up to zero. Each triplet must be unique, and the solution should avoid duplicates. (LeetCode: 3Sum)
Given an array of numbers and a target value, find the triplet whose sum is closest to the target and return that sum. (LeetCode: 3Sum Closest)
Given an array and a target value, count how many triplets have a sum strictly less than the target. (GeeksforGeeks: Count triplets with sum smaller than X)
Given an array of positive numbers and a target, count how many contiguous subarrays have a product strictly less than the target. (LeetCode: Subarray Product Less Than K)
Given an array containing only three distinct values (for example 0, 1, and 2), sort it in place in a single pass without using a counting approach or a library sort. (LeetCode: Sort Colors)
Given an array of numbers and a target, find all unique quadruplets that add up to the target. (LeetCode: 4Sum)

Given two strings that may contain the backspace character (#), determine whether they are equal after applying the backspaces. Aim for a solution with constant extra space. (LeetCode: Backspace String Compare)
Given an array, find the length of the shortest contiguous subarray that, if sorted, would make the entire array sorted in ascending order. (LeetCode: Shortest Unsorted Continuous Subarray)

Given the head of a singly linked list, determine whether the list has a cycle, meaning some node's next pointer points back to an earlier node. Solve it with constant extra space. (LeetCode: Linked List Cycle)
Given the head of a linked list that contains a cycle, return the node where the cycle begins. If there is no cycle, return null. Solve it with constant extra space. (LeetCode: Linked List Cycle II)

A happy number is defined by repeatedly replacing a number with the sum of the squares of its digits; if this process reaches 1 the number is happy, otherwise it loops endlessly. Determine whether a given number is happy. (LeetCode: Happy Number)

Given an array of n plus 1 integers where each integer is between 1 and n inclusive, exactly one number is repeated. Find the duplicate without modifying the array and using only constant extra space. (LeetCode: Find the Duplicate Number)
Given the head of a singly linked list, return the middle node. If there are two middle nodes, return the second one. Solve it in a single pass. (LeetCode: Middle of the Linked List)
Given the head of a singly linked list, determine whether it reads the same forward and backward. Aim for linear time and constant extra space. (LeetCode: Palindrome Linked List)

Given a singly linked list, reorder it so that the nodes interleave from the two ends: the first node, then the last, then the second, then the second-to-last, and so on. Do it in place. (LeetCode: Reorder List)

Given a circular array of non-zero integers where each value tells you how many steps to jump forward (positive) or backward (negative), determine whether there is a cycle. A valid cycle must have all movements in the same direction and a length greater than one. (LeetCode: Circular Array Loop)
Given an array of positive numbers and a window size k, find the maximum sum of any contiguous subarray of exactly k elements. (GeeksforGeeks: Max Sum Subarray of size K)

Given an array of positive numbers and a target sum, find the length of the smallest contiguous subarray whose sum is greater than or equal to the target. If no such subarray exists, return zero. (LeetCode: Minimum Size Subarray Sum)
Given a string and a number k, find the length of the longest substring that contains at most k distinct characters. (GeeksforGeeks: Longest K unique characters substring)

You have two baskets and want to collect fruits from a row of trees, where each basket holds only one type of fruit. Starting from any tree, you must pick from every tree moving right until you cannot. Find the maximum number of fruits you can collect, which equals the longest subarray with at most two distinct values. (LeetCode: Fruit Into Baskets)

Given a string, find the length of the longest substring that contains no repeating characters, using the sliding window pattern. Explain the approach, the data structures, the time and space complexity, and demonstrate it with a complete banking mini-project.

Given a string and an integer k, find the length of the longest substring you can obtain where all characters are the same after replacing at most k characters. Solve it with the sliding window pattern and demonstrate with a complete banking mini-project.

Given a binary array of ones and zeros and an integer k, find the length of the longest contiguous subarray containing only ones after flipping at most k zeros to ones. Solve it with the sliding window pattern and demonstrate with a complete banking mini-project.

Given an array of positive integers and a target value, find the length of the shortest contiguous subarray whose sum is greater than or equal to the target, returning zero if no such subarray exists. Solve it with the sliding window pattern and demonstrate with a complete banking mini-project.

Given a string s and a pattern p, find the smallest substring of s that contains all the characters of p including their required counts, returning an empty result if none exists. Solve it with the sliding window pattern and demonstrate with a complete banking mini-project.

Given a string s and a pattern p, determine whether s contains any permutation of p as a contiguous substring. Solve it with the fixed-size sliding window pattern and demonstrate with a complete banking mini-project.

Given a string s and a pattern p, find the start indices of all substrings of s that are anagrams of p. Solve it with the fixed-size sliding window pattern and demonstrate with a complete banking mini-project.

Given a string s and a list of words all of the same length, find all starting indices in s of substrings that are a concatenation of every word exactly once in any order. Solve it with the sliding window pattern and demonstrate with a complete banking mini-project.

Given an array of integers that may include negative numbers, find the maximum sum obtainable from any contiguous non-empty subarray. Solve it with Kadane's algorithm and demonstrate with a complete banking mini-project.

Given an array of integers that may include positives and negatives, find the minimum sum obtainable from any contiguous non-empty subarray. Solve it with the minimum variant of Kadane's algorithm and demonstrate with a complete banking mini-project.

Given an array of integers that may include negatives and zeros, find the maximum product obtainable from any contiguous non-empty subarray. Solve it with the running max-and-min variant of Kadane's algorithm and demonstrate with a complete banking mini-project.

Given an array of integers that may include negatives, find the maximum sum of a contiguous non-empty subarray where you are allowed to delete at most one element from it. Solve it with a two-state Kadane-style dynamic programming pass and demonstrate with a complete banking mini-project.

Given an array of integers, find the maximum absolute value of the sum of any contiguous non-empty subarray. Solve it by running both maximum and minimum Kadane simultaneously and demonstrate with a complete banking mini-project.

Given a circular array of integers where the end wraps around to the beginning, find the maximum sum of any contiguous non-empty subarray, allowing the subarray to wrap around. Solve it with a combination of maximum and minimum Kadane and demonstrate with a complete banking mini-project.

Given an array of integers that may include negatives and a target value k, find the total number of contiguous subarrays whose elements sum exactly to k. Solve it with the prefix-sum and hash-map pattern and demonstrate with a complete banking mini-project.

Given an array of integers, find the leftmost pivot index where the sum of all elements strictly to its left equals the sum of all elements strictly to its right, returning minus one if no such index exists. Solve it with the prefix-sum pattern and demonstrate with a complete banking mini-project.

Given an array of integers that may include negatives and a positive integer k, count the number of contiguous subarrays whose sum is divisible by k. Solve it with the prefix-sum remainder pattern and demonstrate with a complete banking mini-project.

Given a binary array of zeros and ones, find the length of the longest contiguous subarray that contains an equal number of zeros and ones. Solve it with the prefix-sum and first-occurrence hash-map pattern and demonstrate with a complete banking mini-project.

Given an array of integers that may include negatives and a target k, find the length of the shortest contiguous non-empty subarray whose sum is at least k, returning minus one if none exists. Solve it with prefix sums and a monotonic deque and demonstrate with a complete banking mini-project.

Given an array of integers that may include negatives and two bounds lower and upper, count how many contiguous subarrays have a sum that falls within the inclusive range from lower to upper. Solve it with prefix sums and a merge-sort-based counting technique and demonstrate with a complete banking mini-project.

Given a list of intervals each with a start and an end, merge all overlapping intervals and return the list of non-overlapping intervals that cover the same ranges. Solve it with the sort-then-sweep merge-intervals pattern and demonstrate with a complete banking mini-project.

Given a list of non-overlapping intervals sorted by start and a new interval to insert, insert the new interval and merge any overlaps so the result remains a sorted list of non-overlapping intervals. Solve it with the three-phase merge-intervals pattern and demonstrate with a complete banking mini-project.

Given two lists of closed intervals each sorted by start and internally non-overlapping, return the list of intervals representing their intersection. Solve it with the two-pointer merge-intervals pattern and demonstrate with a complete banking mini-project.

Given a set of intervals each with a start and an end, determine whether any two of them overlap. Solve it with the sort-then-adjacent-check merge-intervals pattern and demonstrate with a complete banking mini-project.

Given an array containing `n` distinct numbers taken from the range `1` to `n` (or `0` to `n-1`), sort the array in place in O(n) time and O(1) extra space without using any sorting library. Explain the Cyclic Sort pattern and where it applies.
Given an array of `n` distinct numbers taken from the range `0` to `n`, exactly one number in that range is missing. Find the missing number in O(n) time and O(1) space.

Given an unsorted array of `n` integers in the range `1` to `n` where some numbers may appear more than once and some numbers are therefore missing, return a list of all the numbers in `1..n` that do not appear. Solve in O(n) time and O(1) extra space (the output list does not count).

Given an array of `n+1` integers where each integer is in the range `1` to `n`, exactly one number is repeated (possibly multiple times). Find the duplicate without modifying the array if required, and discuss both the Cyclic Sort and Floyd's cycle approaches.

Given an array of `n` integers in the range `1` to `n` where some numbers appear once and some appear exactly twice, return all the numbers that appear twice, in O(n) time and O(1) extra space (the output list excluded).

You have an array of `n` numbers that should hold each value `1..n` exactly once, but due to corruption one number got duplicated which caused another number to go missing. Return the pair `[duplicate, missing]` in O(n) time and O(1) space.
Given an unsorted array that may contain duplicates, negatives, and zero, find the smallest positive integer (starting from 1) that does not appear in the array, in O(n) time and O(1) extra space.

Given an unsorted array and a positive integer `k`, return the first `k` missing positive numbers in order. The array may contain duplicates, negatives, and zero. Aim for O(n + k) time and O(k) extra space.
Given the head of a singly linked list, reverse it in place and return the new head. Do it in O(n) time and O(1) extra space.

Given the head of a singly linked list and two positions `p` and `q` (1-based, `p <= q`), reverse the nodes from position `p` to position `q` in place and return the head. Do it in a single pass with O(1) extra space.

Given the head of a singly linked list and a positive integer `k`, reverse every consecutive group of `k` nodes in place and return the new head. If the final group has fewer than `k` nodes, leave it as is. Use O(1) extra space.

Given the head of a singly linked list and a positive integer `k`, reverse every alternate group of `k` nodes in place: reverse the first `k`, skip the next `k`, reverse the following `k`, and so on. Leave any final partial group as is. Use O(1) extra space.

Given the head of a singly linked list and a non-negative integer `k`, rotate the list to the right by `k` places and return the new head. Handle `k` larger than the list length. Use O(1) extra space.
Given the root of a binary tree, return its node values grouped by level, from top to bottom and left to right within each level. Explain the Tree Breadth First Search pattern.
Given the root of a binary tree, return its node values level by level but from the bottom level up to the root, left to right within each level.
Given the root of a binary tree, return its node values in zigzag level order: the first level left to right, the next level right to left, alternating for each subsequent level.
Given the root of a binary tree, return a list containing the average value of the nodes on each level, from top to bottom.
Given the root of a binary tree, find its minimum depth, the number of nodes along the shortest path from the root to the nearest leaf node. A leaf is a node with no children.
Given the root of a binary tree, return its maximum depth, the number of nodes along the longest path from the root down to the farthest leaf.

Given the root of a binary tree and the value of a target node, find its level order successor, the node that appears immediately after the target in a breadth-first traversal. Return null if the target is the last node.
Given a binary tree where each node has an extra `next` pointer, connect each node to its immediate right neighbor on the same level. The last node of each level should point to null.

Given a binary tree with an extra `next` pointer on each node, connect all nodes so that `next` forms a single continuous chain in level order: the last node of each level points to the first node of the next level, not to null.

Given the root of a binary tree, imagine standing on the right side of it; return the values of the nodes visible from the right, ordered top to bottom. This is the last node of each level in a level order traversal.

Given the root of a binary tree, imagine standing on the left side of it; return the values of the nodes visible from the left, ordered top to bottom. This is the first node of each level in a level order traversal.

Given a binary tree and a target sum, determine whether the tree has any root-to-leaf path such that adding up all the node values along the path equals the target sum. Return true or false, and explain why a depth-first traversal is the natural fit for this problem.

Given a binary tree and a target sum, find all root-to-leaf paths where the sum of the node values equals the target. Return the list of paths, and explain how backtracking lets you reuse one working list instead of copying at every node.

Given a binary tree where each node holds a single digit from 0 to 9, each root-to-leaf path represents a number formed by concatenating the digits along the path. Find the total sum of all such numbers, and explain the running-number technique.

Given a binary tree and an array of numbers representing a sequence, determine whether there exists a root-to-leaf path such that the node values along the path exactly match the sequence in order and length. Explain how an index into the sequence tracks progress during the depth-first search.

Given a binary tree and a target sum, count all paths in the tree where the sum of the node values equals the target. The paths do not need to start at the root or end at a leaf, but they must go downward, from a node to one of its descendants. Explain the running-prefix-sum technique that makes this efficient.

Given a binary tree, find its diameter, defined as the number of nodes on the longest path between any two nodes in the tree. The path may or may not pass through the root. Explain why a single post-order traversal that returns subtree heights while updating a global maximum is the efficient solution.

Given a binary tree, find the path with the maximum sum, where a path is any sequence of connected nodes and need not pass through the root or start or end at a leaf. Node values may be negative. Return the maximum path sum, and explain the post-order traversal with a global maximum.

Design a data structure that accepts a continuous stream of numbers and can return the median of all numbers seen so far at any time. Insertion and median-query should both be efficient. Explain the two-heap technique.

Given an array of numbers and a window size K, find the median of every contiguous window of size K as the window slides from left to right. Explain how two heaps with lazy deletion maintain the window median efficiently.

You are given an initial capital and a list of projects, each with a capital requirement and a profit. You can complete at most K projects, and completing a project adds its profit to your capital, which can then fund later projects. Choose projects to maximize final capital. Explain the two-heap greedy approach.

Given an array of intervals, for each interval find the index of the next interval, meaning the interval with the smallest start that is greater than or equal to the current interval's end. If no such interval exists, record -1. Explain how two heaps keyed on start and end solve this efficiently.
Given a set of distinct numbers, generate all possible subsets, including the empty set and the full set. Explain the iterative doubling technique that builds subsets one element at a time.

Given a set of numbers that may contain duplicates, generate all possible unique subsets, with no two subsets identical. Explain how sorting plus a controlled expansion of only the newly added subsets prevents duplicate subsets.
Given a set of distinct numbers, generate all possible permutations, meaning every possible ordering. Explain the backtracking technique that fixes one position at a time.

Given a string with letters and digits, generate all strings that can be formed by changing the case of the letters, leaving digits unchanged. Explain the doubling technique that forks only on letters.
For a given number N, generate all combinations of N pairs of balanced parentheses. Explain the backtracking technique that tracks open and close counts to keep every prefix valid.

Given a word, generate all of its unique generalized abbreviations, where any contiguous run of characters can be replaced by its count. Explain the backtracking choice at each character of keeping it or abbreviating it.

Given a string expression of numbers and the operators plus, minus, and multiply, compute all possible results from different ways of grouping the numbers and operators with parentheses. Explain the divide-and-conquer recursion that splits at each operator.

Given a number N, generate all structurally unique binary search trees that store values 1 through N. Explain how choosing each value as the root and recursively building left and right subtrees enumerates every shape.

Given a number N, count how many structurally unique binary search trees can store values 1 through N, without generating them. Explain the dynamic-programming recurrence derived from choosing each root.

Given a string of digits from 2 to 9, return all possible letter combinations that the digits could represent on a classic phone keypad. Explain the backtracking technique that fixes one digit's letter at a time.

Given a set of distinct positive numbers and a target, find all unique combinations that sum to the target, where each number may be used an unlimited number of times. Explain the backtracking technique with a start index that prevents duplicate combinations.

Given two integers N and K, return all possible combinations of K numbers chosen from the range 1 to N. Explain the backtracking technique with a start index and how to prune when not enough numbers remain.

Given a string, partition it so that every substring of the partition is a palindrome, and return all possible palindrome partitionings. Explain the backtracking technique that cuts the string at each position and only recurses when the prefix is a palindrome.

Given a sorted array of numbers whose sort direction (ascending or descending) is not known in advance, find the index of a target key using binary search. Explain how you detect the order and adjust the comparisons.

Given an array of numbers sorted in ascending order, find the ceiling of a given key, defined as the smallest element greater than or equal to the key. If no such element exists, return minus one. Explain how binary search converges to the ceiling.

Given an array of lowercase letters sorted in ascending order and a target letter, find the smallest letter in the array that is strictly greater than the target. The letters wrap around, so if the target is greater than or equal to the last letter, return the first letter. Explain the binary-search approach.

Given an array of numbers sorted in ascending order, find the range, meaning the first and last index, of a given key. If the key is not present, return minus one for both. Explain how two biased binary searches find the two ends.

Given an infinite sorted array, or one whose length is unknown and can only be probed through an accessor that returns a large sentinel for out-of-bounds indices, find the index of a given key. Explain how you first find a bounding window and then binary-search within it.

Given an array of numbers sorted in ascending order, find the element whose absolute difference from a given key is smallest. If two elements are equally close, return the smaller one. Explain how binary search plus a comparison of the two neighbours around the closing window finds it.

A bitonic array strictly increases to a single maximum and then strictly decreases. Find the maximum value using binary search. Explain how comparing the middle element with its right neighbour tells you which side the peak is on.

Given a bitonic array, strictly increasing then strictly decreasing, find the index of a given key. If the key appears on both sides, return the smaller index. Explain how you first find the peak and then binary-search each side with the correct order.

Given an ascending sorted array that has been rotated at some unknown pivot, find the index of a given key in O(log n). Explain how, at each step, one half of the array is always sorted and how that lets you decide which half to keep.

Given an ascending sorted array that has been rotated an unknown number of times, count how many times it was rotated, which equals the index of its smallest element. Explain how binary search locates the minimum.
In an array where every number appears exactly twice except for one number that appears once, find that single number using constant extra space. Explain why XOR of all elements gives the answer.

In an array where every number appears twice except two numbers that each appear once, find both single numbers using constant extra space. Explain how a distinguishing set bit splits the array into two groups.

Given a positive base-ten integer, find its complement, which is the number formed by flipping every bit in its binary representation, considering only the bits up to and including its highest set bit. Explain how a mask of all ones of the right width makes this a single XOR.

Given a binary matrix, produce a new matrix where each row is first reversed horizontally and then each bit is inverted. Explain how XOR with one performs the inversion and how reversing and inverting can be fused in a single pass.
Given an unsorted array of numbers and a value K, find the K largest numbers. Explain why a min-heap of size K is the efficient structure and how it maintains the K largest seen so far.
Given an unsorted array of numbers and a value K, find the Kth smallest number. Explain how a max-heap of size K keeps the K smallest seen so far, with its root being the answer.

Given a list of points on a plane and a value K, find the K points closest to the origin. Explain how a max-heap keyed on squared distance keeps the K nearest and why squared distance avoids the square root.

Given ropes of different lengths, connecting two ropes costs the sum of their lengths, and the combined rope can be connected again. Find the minimum total cost to connect all ropes into one. Explain why always joining the two shortest ropes is optimal and how a min-heap implements it.
Given an unsorted array of numbers, find the K numbers that appear most frequently. Explain how a frequency map plus a min-heap keyed on frequency finds them efficiently.
Given a string, sort its characters in decreasing order of how often they appear. Explain how a frequency map plus a max-heap keyed on frequency builds the result.

Design a class that, given a value K and an initial list of numbers, returns the Kth largest number each time a new number is added to the stream. Explain how a min-heap of size K supports this efficiently.

Given a sorted array, a target value X, and a count K, find the K numbers closest to X. If two numbers are equally close, prefer the smaller. Explain how binary search locates X and a two-pointer window then selects the K closest.

Given an array of numbers and a value K, you may remove up to K elements. Maximize the number of distinct elements remaining. Explain how a frequency count and a min-heap of the duplicate counts guide which removals help most.

Given an array and two values K1 and K2, find the sum of all elements that are strictly greater than the K1-th smallest and strictly smaller than the K2-th smallest. Explain how two heaps, or finding the two order statistics, let you sum the band in between.

You are given K sorted linked lists. Merge them into a single sorted linked list and return its head. Explain the K-way Merge pattern, the heap-based technique, the time and space complexity, and how it maps to a real banking scenario.
Given M sorted lists of numbers, find the Kth smallest number among all of them. Explain the K-way Merge technique, the heap contents, the complexity, and a banking use case.

Given K sorted integer lists, find the smallest range that includes at least one number from each of the K lists. If several ranges are equally small, return the one with the smaller start. Explain the K-way Merge technique and a banking use case.
Given K sorted arrays, merge them into a single sorted array. Explain the K-way Merge technique with a heap, the complexity, and a banking use case.

Given an N by N matrix where each row and each column is sorted in ascending order, find the Kth smallest element in the matrix. Explain the K-way Merge heap technique, the complexity, and a banking use case.
Given two sorted arrays, find the median of the combined sorted order. Explain how the K-way Merge pattern locates the middle without fully merging, the complexity, and a banking use case.

Given weights and profits of N items, put a subset of these items into a knapsack of capacity C so that the total profit is maximized, where each item can be used at most once. Explain the 0/1 Knapsack dynamic programming pattern, the table, the complexity, and a banking use case.

Given a set of positive numbers, determine if it can be partitioned into two subsets whose sums are equal. Explain how this reduces to 0/1 Knapsack, the DP technique, the complexity, and a banking use case.
Given a set of positive numbers, determine if there is a subset whose sum equals a given target S. Explain the 0/1 Knapsack boolean DP technique, the complexity, and a banking use case.

Given a set of positive numbers, partition them into two subsets so that the absolute difference of their sums is minimized. Return that minimum difference. Explain the 0/1 Knapsack DP technique, the complexity, and a banking use case.
Given a set of positive numbers, count the number of subsets whose sum equals a given target S. Explain the 0/1 Knapsack counting DP technique, the complexity, and a banking use case.

Given a set of positive numbers and a target T, assign a plus or minus sign to each number so that the signed total equals T, and count the number of ways to do so. Explain how this reduces to Count of Subset Sum, the DP technique, the complexity, and a banking use case.

Given weights and profits of N items and a knapsack capacity C, maximize total profit where each item can be used any number of times. Explain the Unbounded Knapsack dynamic programming pattern, how it differs from 0/1, the complexity, and a banking use case.

Given a rod of length N and a list of prices for each length, cut the rod into pieces to maximize total revenue, where each length can be used any number of times. Explain how this is an Unbounded Knapsack, the DP technique, the complexity, and a banking use case.

Given coin denominations and a total amount, count the number of distinct combinations that make up that amount, where each denomination can be used unlimited times. Explain the Unbounded Knapsack counting DP technique, the complexity, and a banking use case.

Given coin denominations and a total amount, find the minimum number of coins needed to make that amount, where each denomination can be used unlimited times. Return minus one if it cannot be made. Explain the Unbounded Knapsack minimization DP technique, the complexity, and a banking use case.

Given a ribbon of length N and a set of allowed cut lengths, cut the ribbon into the maximum number of pieces using only allowed lengths, where each length can be used unlimited times. Return minus one if the ribbon cannot be cut exactly. Explain the Unbounded Knapsack maximization-count DP, the complexity, and a banking use case.

Compute the Nth Fibonacci number, where each number is the sum of the two preceding ones. Explain the Fibonacci Numbers dynamic programming pattern, bottom-up versus memoization, the complexity, and a banking use case.

Given a staircase of N steps, count the number of distinct ways to reach the top if you can take one, two, or three steps at a time. Explain the Fibonacci Numbers DP pattern, the recurrence, the complexity, and a banking use case.

Given a number N, count the number of distinct ways to express it as an ordered sum using only the factors one, three, and four. Explain the Fibonacci Numbers DP pattern, the recurrence, the complexity, and a banking use case.

Given an array where each element is the maximum jump length from that position, find the minimum number of jumps to reach the last index from the first. Explain the Fibonacci Numbers DP pattern view, the recurrence, the complexity, and a banking use case.

Given an array of fees where each index charges a fee to step on it, and you may climb one or two steps at a time starting before the first step, find the minimum total fee to reach the top past the last step. Explain the Fibonacci Numbers DP pattern, the recurrence, the complexity, and a banking use case.

Given an array of non-negative numbers representing the value in each house along a street, find the maximum total you can collect without taking from two adjacent houses. Explain the Fibonacci Numbers DP pattern, the recurrence, the complexity, and a banking use case.

Given a staircase of N steps, count the number of distinct ways to climb to the top if you can take one or two steps at a time. Explain the Fibonacci Numbers DP pattern, why the answer is a Fibonacci number, the complexity, and a banking use case.

Given a string, find the length of its longest palindromic subsequence, where a subsequence keeps relative order but need not be contiguous. Explain the Palindromic Subsequence DP pattern, the recurrence, the complexity, and a banking use case.

Given a string, find the length of its longest palindromic substring, where a substring must be contiguous. Explain the Palindromic Subsequence DP pattern applied to contiguous ranges, the recurrence, the complexity, and a banking use case.

Given a string, count how many of its contiguous substrings are palindromes, counting each position separately even if the content repeats. Explain the Palindromic Subsequence DP pattern applied to counting, the recurrence, the complexity, and a banking use case.

Given a string, find the minimum number of character deletions needed to make it a palindrome. Explain how the Palindromic Subsequence DP pattern solves it, the recurrence, the complexity, and a banking use case.

Given a string, find the minimum number of cuts needed so that every resulting piece is a palindrome. Explain how the Palindromic Subsequence pattern combines with a cut dynamic program, the recurrence, the complexity, and a banking use case.

Given a string, find the minimum number of characters you must insert anywhere to make it a palindrome. Explain how the Palindromic Subsequence pattern solves it, the recurrence, the complexity, and a banking use case.

Given two strings, find the length of the longest substring that appears in both, where a substring must be contiguous. Explain the Longest Common Substring DP pattern, the recurrence, the complexity, and a banking use case.

Given two strings, find the length of the longest subsequence common to both, where a subsequence keeps relative order but need not be contiguous. Explain the Longest Common Substring DP pattern applied to subsequences, the recurrence, the complexity, and a banking use case.

Given two strings, find the minimum number of deletions and insertions needed to transform the first string into the second, using only deletions and insertions. Explain how the Longest Common Substring pattern solves it through the longest common subsequence, the recurrence, the complexity, and a banking use case.

Given an array of numbers, find the length of the longest strictly increasing subsequence, where a subsequence keeps relative order but need not be contiguous. Explain the Longest Common Substring pattern connection, the recurrence, the complexity, and a banking use case.

Given an array of numbers, find the maximum sum of any strictly increasing subsequence. Explain how the Longest Increasing Subsequence dynamic program adapts to maximise sum instead of length, the recurrence, the complexity, and a banking use case.

Given two strings, find the length of the shortest string that has both of them as subsequences. Explain how the Longest Common Substring pattern through the longest common subsequence solves it, the recurrence, the complexity, and a banking use case.

Given two strings, find the minimum number of single-character insertions, deletions, and substitutions needed to transform the first into the second. Explain the Edit Distance dynamic program within the Longest Common Substring pattern family, the recurrence, the complexity, and a banking use case.

Given a directed acyclic graph of dependencies, produce a linear ordering of the nodes such that every edge points from an earlier node to a later node. Explain the Topological Sort pattern using Kahn's algorithm, the recurrence, the complexity, and a banking use case.

Given a number of tasks and a list of prerequisite pairs, determine whether it is possible to finish all tasks. Explain how the Topological Sort pattern decides feasibility, the recurrence, the complexity, and a banking use case.

Given a number of tasks and prerequisite pairs, return one valid order in which all tasks can be completed, or an empty result if no such order exists. Explain how the Topological Sort pattern produces the order, the recurrence, the complexity, and a banking use case.

Given a number of tasks and prerequisite pairs, enumerate every valid order in which all tasks can be completed. Explain how the Topological Sort pattern combines with backtracking, the recurrence, the complexity, and a banking use case.

Given a list of words sorted according to an unknown alphabet, derive a valid ordering of the characters in that alphabet. Explain how the Topological Sort pattern solves it, the recurrence, the complexity, and a banking use case.

Given a number of courses and prerequisite pairs, determine whether the dependency graph contains a cycle, using a depth-first colouring approach. Explain this depth-first variant of the Topological Sort pattern, the recurrence, the complexity, and a banking use case.

Implement a trie, also called a prefix tree, supporting inserting a word, searching for a complete word, and checking whether any word starts with a given prefix. Explain the Trie pattern, the operations, the complexity, and a banking use case.

Given a grid of characters and a set of dictionary words, find all dictionary words that can be formed by a path of adjacent cells without reusing a cell. Explain how the Trie pattern accelerates the search, the recurrence, the complexity, and a banking use case.

Given a list of words, find the longest word that can be built one character at a time, where every prefix of that word is also present in the list; break ties by taking the smallest word in dictionary order. Explain how the Trie pattern solves it, the recurrence, the complexity, and a banking use case.

Given a set of root words and a sentence, replace every word in the sentence with the shortest root that is a prefix of it, leaving words with no matching root unchanged. Explain how the Trie pattern solves it, the recurrence, the complexity, and a banking use case.

Given a set of words and a typed prefix, return all words that start with that prefix, optionally limited to the top few. Explain how the Trie pattern provides autocomplete, the operations, the complexity, and a banking use case.

Given n cities, a list of flights as (from, to, price), a source, a destination, and a maximum number of stops K, find the cheapest price to reach the destination using at most K stops. Explain the Bellman-Ford style relaxation, the operations, the complexity, and a banking use case.

Given a connected weighted undirected graph, find the minimum spanning tree — the subset of edges that connects every vertex with the smallest total weight. Explain Prim's algorithm with a priority queue, the operations, the complexity, and a banking use case.

Given a begin word, an end word, and a dictionary of equal-length words, find the length of the shortest transformation sequence that changes one letter at a time, where every intermediate word must be in the dictionary. Explain the breadth-first search solution, the operations, the complexity, and a banking use case.

Compute the nth Fibonacci number, where each number is the sum of the two before it. Explain the naive recursion, why it is slow, how memoization and the bottom-up rolling approach fix it, the complexity, and a banking use case.

You climb a staircase of n steps, and at each move you take either one step or two steps. Count the number of distinct ways to reach the top. Explain the dynamic programming recurrence, the operations, the complexity, and a banking use case.

Given an array of non-negative values, pick a subset with the maximum total such that no two picked elements are adjacent. Explain the dynamic programming recurrence, the operations, the complexity, and a banking use case.

Given items each with a weight and a value, and a knapsack capacity, choose a subset to maximise total value without exceeding the capacity, where each item is taken at most once. Explain the top-down memoized recursion, the operations, the complexity, and a banking use case.
Explain the concept of tabulation in dynamic programming — how it differs from memoization, how you fill a table from base cases upward, the trade-offs, the complexity, and a banking use case.

Solve the 0/1 Knapsack problem bottom-up with a table instead of recursion, then reduce the table to a single row. Explain the recurrence, the reverse-capacity iteration, the operations, the complexity, and a banking use case.

Given an array of non-negative integers and a target, determine whether any subset sums exactly to the target. Explain the dynamic programming boolean table, the reverse-iteration single-row optimisation, the complexity, and a banking use case.

Given an array of non-negative integers and a target, count the number of ways to assign a plus or minus sign to each number so the signed sum equals the target. Explain the reduction to a subset-count problem, the dynamic programming, the complexity, and a banking use case.

Given an array of numbers, find the length of the longest strictly increasing subsequence, where the chosen elements keep their original order but need not be contiguous. Explain the quadratic dynamic programming and the optimal patience-sorting approach, the complexity, and a banking use case.

Explain the classic quadratic bottom-up tabulation for the Longest Increasing Subsequence, how each cell is built from earlier cells, how to reconstruct the actual subsequence with predecessor pointers, the complexity, and a banking use case.

Given two sequences, find the length of the longest subsequence common to both, preserving order but not requiring contiguity. Explain the two-dimensional dynamic programming, the row-rolling optimisation, the complexity, and a banking use case.

Count the number of distinct paths from the top-left to the bottom-right of an m by n grid, moving only right or down. Explain the dynamic programming recurrence, the single-row optimisation, the complexity, and a banking use case.

Given daily prices, maximise profit from buying and selling a stock, covering the single-transaction case and the unlimited-transaction case. Explain both algorithms, the operations, the complexity, and a banking use case.

Given a stick of length L and a set of positions where it must be cut, where each cut costs the length of the piece being cut, find the minimum total cost to make all cuts in any order. Explain the interval dynamic programming, the operations, the complexity, and a banking use case.

Summarise how to recognise a dynamic programming problem and how to frame its state and transition. Explain optimal substructure, overlapping subproblems, the standard patterns, the memoization-versus-tabulation choice, and a banking use case.

Customers pay with 5, 10, or 20 unit notes for a 5 unit item and you start with no change. Determine whether you can give correct change to every customer in order. Explain the greedy strategy, the operations, the complexity, and a banking use case.

Given an array where each value is the maximum jump length from that index, determine whether you can reach the last index starting from the first. Explain the greedy farthest-reach approach, the operations, the complexity, and a banking use case.

Each child has a greed factor and each cookie has a size; a child is content only if a cookie's size meets or exceeds the child's greed. Maximise the number of content children. Explain the greedy two-pointer approach, the operations, the complexity, and a banking use case.

What is AWS, and what is the difference between a Region, an Availability Zone (AZ), and an Edge Location?
What is IAM, and what is the difference between an IAM User, an IAM Group, an IAM Role, and an IAM Policy?

What is the difference between authentication and authorization in IAM, and how does policy evaluation work (explicit deny > explicit allow > implicit deny)?
What is the principle of least privilege, and how do you scope a policy to a single resource (e.g. grant access to only one S3 bucket or one ECR repository)?

What is EC2, what are instance families/types (general purpose, compute/memory/storage optimized), and what parameters do you consider when launching an instance (AMI, instance type, key pair, security group, subnet, IAM role, storage)?
What is a key pair in EC2, and how do you connect to a Linux instance (SSH with the private key) vs a Windows instance?
What is a Security Group, how does it differ from a Network ACL (stateful instance-level allow-only vs stateless subnet-level allow+deny), and when do you use each?
